book.title: Execution: The Discipline of Getting Things Done
book.author: Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan

chapters.title: The Gap Nobody Knows
chapters.hook: Turnaround lead Eleanor stops in the doorway and asks which line almost broke.
chapters.counterintuition: The gap opens after the strategy sounds settled. You find it by making the person, the bet, and the path answer to proof that can come back.
chapters.tryThisNow: On your next status call, count for 5 minutes how many promises name a person and a return; write the first blank you saw.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not bless a goal until the capable person, the strategic bet, and the operating path can be counted against proof that returns soon.

breakdown.fastRead:
Turnaround lead Eleanor stops in the doorway after the goal holds. Everyone wants to leave with the win, but she asks which line almost broke. The win can be the place where the miss was hiding.

A health insurer gives the first plain case: a recovery story can run ahead of what the business can prove. Aetna's 2000 leadership change shows why the old record has to be faced before a turnaround claim can hold. If you look only at strategy, you miss who must carry it. If you look only at staffing, you miss the bet. If you look only at operations, you miss why the path matters. Put the three answers in one count. Then a promise has a person, proof, and a return.
breakdown.deepRead:
A promise becomes real when a named person, a visible proof point, and a return sit in the same ledger. Without that count, intent can sound firm while no one knows what would prove it false.

A copier company under cash and trust pressure gives the second case. Xerox's 2001 leadership crisis showed cash, debt, and customer trust pressing at the same time. Customer lead Blake can name the cash path and the debt path, yet still leave trust outside the count. Eleanor hears the blank and asks, "Which line is soft?" Blake says, "Trust." That answer changes the diagnosis.

The hard part is not the word trust. The hard part is making trust answer beside cash and debt, rather than treating it as a soft feeling that will fix itself after the money path improves. When the soft line stays off the ledger, the senior team can believe the crisis is smaller than it is.

Senior managers create the gap when they hand the hard part down after the broad goal sounds strong. Staff can gather detail. They cannot replace the duty to surface reality, name who returns, and make the missing proof visible before pride hardens around the story.

Which hidden line would make the promise false if it surfaced today? Ask before the next pass, not after the miss. Early bad data is not betrayal. It is the first clean signal that the promise can still be changed.
breakdown.fullRead:
A telecom equipment company makes the trap look strong at first. Lucent Technologies became a separate telecom equipment business in 1996; later, a telecom collapse exposed weak revenue, cost, and forecasting. Fast market growth had made the business look sounder than its habits.

That is why diagnosis has to hold three fields at once. People answers who has the judgment and duty to carry the promise. Strategy answers what bet is being made. Operations answers how strain will show soon. Leave one field out, and the other two can sound better than they are.

Aetna brings the inherited record. Xerox brings cash, debt, and customer trust at once. Lucent brings the false comfort of growth. The cases are not a stack of warnings. They show the same blank at different doors: the business stated intent, then results asked who would carry it.

Eleanor uses a simple ledger, not a longer form. What does the business already know? Who is close enough to return with proof? Which bet is this result meant to serve? A vague answer can be honest when it comes back soon. A vague answer that never returns is cover.

Count the promise before you trust it. A goal can gather nods because it does not yet ask anyone to give up a favored option, admit a bad forecast, or bring back proof. Once the return is named, the same goal becomes smaller and more useful.

This is also a senior duty. The top group cannot send the hard part below and call that delegation. It has to make hidden data speak early, because every later choice depends on what is real. If bad signals are punished, the ledger goes quiet when it should get loud.

The method has a plain sound when it works. One person says what could make the target false. Another says when the answer comes back. Someone else names the path that will show strain first. A bystander would not hear theater. They would hear a promise being made small enough to test.

Use the full scan when the promise matters, the cost of being wrong is high, or a broad goal has started to feel safer than proof. Do the opposite for small, reversible choices. It costs time and candor. It can slow a trial that should run fast. Do not turn it into theater. A tiny trial needs speed more than a full ledger, and a low-risk choice can teach faster by being tried. When stakes are low, try the thing and learn. When the promise can hurt cash, customers, or trust, make people, strategy, and operations answer in one count.

examples.title: Eleanor Finds The Late Blank
examples.scenario: The hallway light buzzes as turnaround lead Eleanor looks back across the target that just held. A health insurer still has to face its inherited record before the recovery story can hold. Aetna's 2000 leadership change shows old performance proof comes first. Eleanor finds the line late, and the story survives barely.
examples.whatToDo: Trace the miss backward. Name who saw the inherited record and which return would have exposed it before the story hardened.
examples.whyItMatters: Count the blank early. A recovery claim is still soft when the known record has no person, no return, and no way to be tested soon.

examples.title: Blake Names Trust Last
examples.scenario: Customer lead Blake enters the cash pass and names the part the room left outside: debt has names, cost has a path, and customer trust has only hope. Treat the company as fighting money pressure and credibility at once. Xerox's 2001 leadership crisis shows why cash, debt, and customer trust have to answer together. The move half-works; trust stays broken.
examples.whatToDo: Treat trust as a live line. Give it a person and a return beside cash and debt in the same pass, not after money feels tidy.
examples.whyItMatters: Keep the soft line in the count. You cannot repair a crisis by solving the part that is easiest to measure and leaving trust vague.

examples.title: Eleanor Prices Growth
examples.scenario: The cost is already forming before anyone notices: growth looks strong while revenue, cost, and forecasts do not balance. Turnaround lead Eleanor sees it inside a telecom equipment business riding a fast market. Lucent Technologies became separate in 1996; later collapse exposed those weak spots. The marker squeaks once. Eleanor names the gap, and the favored growth claim loses cover.
examples.whatToDo: Price the lost signal before scale flatters the group. Make revenue, cost, and forecast habits answer while the market still looks kind.
examples.whyItMatters: Face the cost of skipping it. Growth can make weak habits look strong until the market turns and proof is no longer cheap.

examples.title: Aaron Sets The Standard
examples.scenario: The mechanism is blunt: no goal closes on target alone, operations lead Aaron says when the room asks for the standard. Aetna in 2000, Xerox in 2001, and Lucent Technologies after 1996 show the same pattern once strategy is stated. Results expose whether people, proof, and a return exist. The first version is headed for a miss. A person is named late, proof is made visible late, and the catch is just enough.
examples.whatToDo: Force proof early because results will ask the question later. Then name the person and return before agreement is counted.
examples.whyItMatters: Catch the miss before language hardens. The standard works because it makes the goal answerable while a repair is still possible.

examples.title: Blake Sets The Return
examples.scenario: Can cash improve while trust stays blank? Yes, and customer lead Blake is already counting that danger while the company works through cash and credibility pressure. Xerox's 2001 leadership crisis shows cash, debt, and customer trust pressing at the same time. A phone vibrates once. Cash has a path, debt has a path, and trust has a return. The answer is not met yet.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the live question: can money improve while trust stays blank? Answer by setting a return for trust before cash owns the whole story.
examples.whyItMatters: Answer the doubt plainly. Cash and debt can move while customer trust remains unresolved, so trust needs its own line back.

examples.title: Ethan Brings Growth Back
examples.scenario: At the return, forecast lead Ethan asks whether rapid market growth proved strength or hid weak discipline. Lucent Technologies became a separate telecom equipment business in 1996, and later market collapse exposed revenue, cost, and forecasting weakness. Ethan gives up the easy scale claim. The move works, but status is the price.
examples.whatToDo: Separate market lift from business strength. Make the growth claim answer to revenue, cost, and forecast habits before scale earns credit.
examples.whyItMatters: Protect the count. Scale can flatter a weak system until the market stops helping and the late return costs status for the group.

questions.prompt: A rescue effort worked once after Aaron stayed late and pushed across the line. A month later, the same miss shows up again. Which next move would have kept the pattern from repeating?
choices: Tie rewards to the last person who saved the month, using that save as proof the operating pattern is strong for the group.
Build a repeatable pass where behavior, proof, and consequences are read together before pressure peaks again at month end.
Rewrite the culture language after the miss, so people hear the expected behavior before any result is due across the cycle.
questions.explanation: b is right: a one-time rescue teaches little unless behavior and evidence recur. a tempts because the save was real, but it treats a late push as proof.

questions.prompt: A health insurer names a new recovery story while the inherited record stays off to the side. What is actually wrong?
choices: The new leader's style should be judged first, since personality will show whether the recovery story can travel.
The old performance record has to be faced before the recovery claim can carry weight with the senior team.
The story can be accepted once the new lead sounds clear enough to separate past from future pressure.
questions.explanation: b fits the Aetna lesson: the inherited record comes before the turnaround claim. a is close only if style is the problem, but the case asks for proof.

questions.prompt: Your unit has a staffing answer, a market bet, and a delivery path, but each is discussed in a separate pass. What should you do next?
choices: Put the three answers in one diagnosis and ask where the person, bet, and path do not match under pressure today.
Narrow the pass to delivery first, since operating strain is the clearest proof that the goal might fail this month.
Wait for the market result, then bring staffing into the later pass if the bet has already shown enough promise.
questions.explanation: a is the taught move: diagnose the linked parts together. b sounds practical, but it narrows the scope and leaves staffing and the bet outside.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit adopts a bold goal and leaves the return point unnamed because the team wants energy first. What happens downstream?
choices: The due line can be added after the first results, once the team sees which part needs pressure.
The broad goal will be enough if senior people repeat it consistently across the first cycle with care.
The goal stays soft because no person owes a near result that others can read later together in time.
questions.explanation: c is right: aspiration without a return stays loose. a is the tempting delay, but the return is what makes the goal answerable early.

questions.prompt: Early warning signs reach a sponsor, and she treats them as disloyal before the path is set. Which diagnosis fits?
choices: The first job is to bring the hard signal into view before later choices lean on a false base.
The warning should be filtered by a support group, so senior time stays focused on final answers.
The sponsor should wait for a full-cycle result, since early strain can make a sound goal look weak to others.
questions.explanation: a fits: hidden data blocks later calls. c feels cautious, but waiting changes an early signal into a late cost.

questions.prompt: The target failed after senior managers handed the hard part to staff once the goal sounded persuasive. Which earlier step was the cause?
choices: Senior managers stayed too close to delivery, so staff lacked space to adapt the broad goal.
The top group treated delivery as someone else's job instead of owning person, proof, and return.
Staff did not write enough process detail before the senior group moved to the next target.
questions.explanation: b matches the cause: senior managers made the gap by delegating the hard part. c sounds orderly, but more detail below cannot replace top duty.

questions.prompt: Three companies state a strategy, then customers, staff, and financial results tell a different story. What is the real problem?
choices: The message has not reached enough people, so the sponsor should make the statement clearer across the business.
The plan should be narrowed to finance alone, since results are the only hard evidence the group can trust.
Results are exposing a loose promise after the statement, so diagnosis has to become measurable and correctable.
questions.explanation: c captures the pattern across Aetna, Xerox, and Lucent. a tempts because clarity helps, but the issue is delivered results, not wording.

questions.prompt: Lucent grows quickly, and Ethan accepts scale as proof that revenue, cost, and forecasts are sound. What is likely being missed?
choices: Fast demand may be covering weak habits in revenue, cost, and forecasting before anyone notices them.
Scale is enough evidence for now, because a growing market shows the business can carry its path.
The only issue is whether leaders named the market earlier, not whether the operating lines balance as a group.
questions.explanation: a follows the Lucent warning: market lift can mask weak habits. b accepts scale as proof, which is the very error the case blocks.

questions.prompt: Xerox has cash pressure and debt pressure, and customer trust is left as a soft topic. Which move best fits?
choices: Work the debt path first, then bring customer trust back once money pressure eases for the group.
Accept a clean financial pass if the cash and debt lines can be explained clearly enough.
Read cash, debt, and trust as live tests together, with a return for each line in the same pass.
questions.explanation: c fits Xerox: the money lines and trust press at once. a is tempting under cash stress, but it leaves one live test outside the diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: What gap should a senior team look for after strategy sounds settled?
reviewCards.back: Look for the distance between the promise and what customers, staff, and money lines feel. A real answer names the person, proof, and return.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Aetna case start with inherited performance proof?
reviewCards.back: Aetna's 2000 change shows that a recovery story cannot outrun the old record. The record must be faced before the story can hold.

reviewCards.front: What does Xerox add to the diagnosis?
reviewCards.back: Xerox shows that cash, debt, and customer trust can press at the same time. Solving only the clean money line leaves the crisis partly unnamed.

reviewCards.front: What does Lucent Technologies after 1996 warn against?
reviewCards.back: Lucent Technologies warns against treating fast market growth as proof of strength. Revenue, cost, and forecast habits still have to answer when the market is kind.

reviewCards.front: How do senior managers create the gap?
reviewCards.back: They create it when they hand delivery down after the goal sounds persuasive. Staff can help gather proof, but the top group still owns the hard call.

reviewCards.front: Why does an aspiration need a return point?
reviewCards.back: A return point makes the goal answerable. It also brings hidden data forward while the group can still change the person, the bet, or the path.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Count whether a goal has three lines: person, proof, and return. Then ask whether the staffing choice, strategic bet, and operating path balance. If one line is blank, keep the goal as a draft and set the smallest return that could expose drift.

ifThenPlans.context: After a goal sounds agreed and before people leave
ifThenPlans.plan: If a goal sounds agreed, then count the person and the return, then ask which proof would make it false.

ifThenPlans.context: After growth looks strong and before you accept scale as proof
ifThenPlans.plan: If growth looks strong, then compare it with revenue, cost, and forecast habits, then name the line that does not balance.

ifThenPlans.context: After an early bad signal appears and before pride settles
ifThenPlans.plan: If a bad signal appears early, then write what it could change, then bring it back before the target hardens.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During tomorrow's morning calendar scan, count live promises for 10 minutes; mark one that lacks a person or return and raise that blank before noon.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Before the weekly planning pass you already attend, if one live goal in your task list lacks person, proof, or return, then write the missing line and bring it to that pass.

Count the promise before you trust it.

chapters.title: The Execution Difference
chapters.hook: A merger does not make a business better; the first hard ask can.
chapters.counterintuition: The bold move feels decisive because the chart changes. The gap opens afterward, when no one can say who owes which number and where the answer will be read.
chapters.tryThisNow: Set a 60-second timer and say this out loud about one live promise: Who owes which number by which day, and who will ask for it?
chapters.keyTakeaway: A structural move pays off only when you attach it to a named person, a measured result, and a return habit that brings weak assumptions into view.

breakdown.fastRead:
A merger does not make a business better. The Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger created a combined industrial company, yet the close only made a new shape; it did not prove that the shape would deliver.

Start after the deal, not at the signing. AT&T split off Lucent Technologies in 1996; Lucent was a telecom gear company facing spending cycles. A split can be neat and still thin. The hard sentence comes after the chart changes: one person owes one number, and the same table asks again.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is plain: a promise has to answer in a form the business can see. If the line says only "improve the launch," everyone can nod and keep moving. If the line says a named person owes a measured answer by a stated day, the gap has a place to show up. A deadline is not a calendar square; it is the place where a promise answers.

Do not put the full version of this move on every small choice. If a low-risk call can be reversed soon, run a short trial with one guardrail and learn from it. If a true emergency is still unstable, act first and sort the ledger after the danger drops. The method costs time and candor, so use the lighter trial when the price of being wrong is small and the learning comes fast.

General Electric (1981 to 2001 chief executive era) gives the repeat case. Its management reviews and talent assessment made return less dependent on mood. The useful part is not the famous name at the top; the useful part is the demand for business detail. Which assumption could fail? Which person has the skill? Which barrier has to move before the number can change?

This is not micromanagement. The senior person does not take over every task. They ask the question that tests the guess, then remove the block the team cannot remove alone. Scale can fool you here. Growth may hide a weak path until the miss is large.

The Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger shows why the close is only the start for a combined industrial company. A deal can join the parts of a company while the actual handoffs stay vague. The better pass asks whether people, strategy, and operations can face the same number. What changed after the first yes? That is where the lesson lives.
breakdown.fullRead:
AT&T separated Lucent Technologies in 1996. Lucent was a telecom equipment company exposed to capital-cycle pressure, which means the new business had to live with swings in equipment investment. The structural act was real. It still did not prove that the pressure had been turned into a due answer.

That is the warning. A split, merger, budget shift, or new unit can look brave because the chart changes. The chart changes first; the business changes only when the number comes back. If no one has to bring back the market fact, the staffing risk, and the operating result together, the new shape has no way to correct itself.

The Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger supplies the before-after ledger. Before the combination is tested, the page says the deal closed and the combined industrial company exists. After the first hard ask, the same page has a person, a due day, a number, and a barrier. The delta is not theatrical. The delta is that the business can now see where the promise is thin.

This is why the senior job cannot be handed to staff once the sentence sounds good. You do not need title power to use the move. On your own project, ask the small version: Who owes me what by when, and what number will show whether it worked? If the answer embarrasses the promise, the question helped.

Dialogue matters because it lets the weak part appear before the customer pays for it. Curtis may hear a sharp debate between two functions and want to smooth it out. Smoothing is not the job. The job is to ask which assumption the argument has exposed, then put that assumption where it can return with an answer.

Rewards teach the same rule. If praise follows the clean account, the careful doer learns to sell the story first. If praise follows what came back, others copy that. Culture does not change because a phrase improves. It changes when the visible reward tells people which behavior counts.

General Electric adds durability. In the 1981 to 2001 chief executive era, General Electric is useful here because repeated reviews made follow-through institutional. One hard pass can catch a miss. A steady cadence teaches what kind of answer counts before the miss gets big.

The danger is overuse. A person who turns every tiny choice into a formal line will slow the group and call it discipline. That is not the lesson. Use the hard version when a structural move, a material promise, or a cross-functional handoff can hide the gap. Use the lighter trial when the call is reversible and the learning comes soon.

AT&T/Lucent is the warning; Honeywell/Alliedsignal is the working case. One shows that a clean separation still needs due answers. The other shows why a post-close habit can make the deal visible. Skipping the ask buys speed and pays it back as drift. The cost is late correction, repeated debate, and rewards that teach the wrong lesson.

examples.title: The Unchanged Promise
examples.scenario: At the moment the post-close standard is stated, merger lead Walker has the Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger in a before line and an after line. Before: the combined industrial company has a deal promise. After Walker lets the demand pass without naming a due answer, the same promise returns unchanged. The miss lands quietly: no unit can say who owes the number, so the standard has no bite.
examples.whatToDo: When skipping the line would save time, make the cost explicit. Walker names the person, result, and due day before the merger promise can count.
examples.whyItMatters: When the miss returns unchanged, speed has turned into rework. The close cannot teach the business what to do until the answer has to come back.

examples.title: Annabelle Pays In Hours
examples.scenario: Midstream, operating lead Annabelle is already paying the cost. The broad target was set earlier; now she is using the General Electric benchmark from the 1981 to 2001 chief executive era. She asks the business detail first, then matches skill to the weak line, then sets the return. It works because the pass repeats, but the price is hours of close attention.
examples.whatToDo: When repetition is already costing hours, use the cost well: ask which business detail could break the claim, then match a capable person to it.
examples.whyItMatters: When the broad target sounds persuasive, repeated passes keep it from becoming staff drift. The habit works because the answer must return.

examples.title: Curtis Finds The Blank
examples.scenario: Can the split still miss after the separation is done? Separation lead Curtis is at the return moment for AT&T's 1996 separation of Lucent Technologies, the telecom equipment company exposed to capital-cycle pressure. A pen stops above the blank line. He has to decide whether ambition counts or the blank line blocks the split.
examples.whatToDo: When the blank line appears late, answer it directly: name the pressure, the person, and the measured answer before ambition counts.
examples.whyItMatters: If the shape is already set, the late catch still matters. The pressure cannot be managed by a braver sentence.

examples.title: Winnie Leaves It Open
examples.scenario: After the miss, operating lead Winnie traces the Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger backward. The combined industrial company did not have one bad sentence; it had three clean lanes that never faced the same number. Staffing sounded ready, strategy sounded clear, and operations stayed soft. The return is now set, but no answer has come back.
examples.whatToDo: When lanes split, set one return across them. Winnie names the person, the number, and the unresolved risk in a single sentence.
examples.whyItMatters: If the answer is absent, leave it open. A linked question beats three clean claims that never have to face one number.

examples.title: Walker Hears Credit Move
examples.scenario: Outside the operating session, senior lead Walker hears the change first: praise follows the delivered result, not the smooth account. The hallway is cold. In the Alliedsignal-Honeywell 1999 merger case, the combined industrial company pays a status cost when the favored claim loses weight. The move works because the reward tells others what to copy.
examples.whatToDo: When praise follows the account, move it. Attach credit to the delivered result and name the person who brought it back.
examples.whyItMatters: When others copy rewards, teach them with the reward. Do not let culture words outrun the behavior that actually returned.

questions.prompt: Curtis approves a separate Lucent unit and leaves the operating asks for later. What happens downstream?
choices: The new structure should be judged mainly by cleaner focus; due answers can wait until the cycle shows stress later.
The sponsor can set a market-pressure target now and let each function decide later who brings the first answer.
The split remains unproved until a named person must return a measured answer tied to that pressure on a set day.
questions.explanation: The separation is not the result. The cleaner-focus choice waits for pressure to show itself, but the operating demand asks for an answer while the pressure can still be managed.

questions.prompt: Annabelle hears a target that sounds strong, but she knows none of the business detail. Which principle is at risk?
choices: She should score the speaker's confidence first, since style can reveal whether people and strategy are lined up.
She should accept the target for now, then ask staff for detail once the broad direction is settled.
She should learn enough of the business to ask which assumption, number, or barrier would change the call.
questions.explanation: The principle is close knowledge. Confidence scoring sounds linked to people and strategy, yet it swaps business detail for style and cannot test the target.

questions.prompt: Winnie separates staffing, strategy, and operating numbers into clean lanes, then gains fade. What best explains why?
choices: Early bad signals arrived before the lanes were ready, so she should have waited for finished answers before joining them.
The gains did not last because the people choice, strategic bet, and operating number never had to answer together.
The first pass was too narrow, so more scale would have proved strength once the signals grew large enough.
questions.explanation: Durability comes from forcing the lanes to face the same answer. Waiting for finished answers treats early bad signals as a nuisance instead of usable data.

questions.prompt: Walker sees scale improve and starts taking over each task himself. Which correction fits here?
choices: He should take over only the weak tasks, since assumption testing works best when the sponsor controls the details.
He should test the shaky assumption and remove the barrier while the task stays with the person doing it.
He should step back because growth is already the clearest sign that the operating path is strong.
questions.explanation: The distinction separates testing from takeover. The scale option is tempting because it looks like proof, but growth can hide a weak path.

questions.prompt: Annabelle schedules one intense GE-style pass after a broad goal sounds persuasive. What is missing?
choices: The pass has to repeat until returning with proof becomes part of the management habit, not a burst of attention.
The first pass should be enough if staff own the details after the goal has been made persuasive and visible.
The pass should wait until the goal is failing, because repetition before a miss slows the business and blurs focus.
questions.explanation: GE adds cadence. Staff detail can help, but handing the goal off after one strong pass stops before the habit forms.

questions.prompt: Walker praises the clean account before the delivered result is known. What behavior will the better reward rule teach?
choices: It will teach people to pair strong accounts with later results, so culture language carries behavior until proof arrives.
It will teach people to wait for perfect comparisons, even when delivered promises vanish in the delay.
It will teach people that credit follows the result that came back, not the account that sounded best first.
questions.explanation: Rewards teach what gets copied. Waiting for perfect comparison sounds careful, but it lets the delivered result lose force while people learn delay.

questions.prompt: Curtis delays hard debate until a customer complaint confirms the weak assumption. What did he misunderstand?
choices: Debate should begin when the due day is missed, because pressure is the clean signal for naming who answers.
Honest argument is useful earlier, when it exposes a weak assumption before the customer carries the cost.
Debate should stay broad enough to protect flexibility, because naming the assumption too soon narrows choices.
questions.explanation: Dialogue is an early warning device. The due-day option starts the argument after the outside cost has arrived, which is late for this move.

questions.prompt: Walker treats the Honeywell-Alliedsignal close as a communication problem and rewrites the message. What consequence follows?
choices: The deal still lacks a post-close habit that makes each promise measurable, correctable, and due back.
The clearer message should solve the drift if every function hears the same post-close language.
The deal should be left informal after close, since new units need freedom before they owe numbers to anyone.
questions.explanation: The Honeywell-Alliedsignal case is about discipline after close. Clearer language is plausible, but it leaves no recurring way to measure and correct.

questions.prompt: Winnie brings a tidy plan with no named person, due day, or measured result. Which priority comes first?
choices: Make the plan usable by naming the person, the measured result, and when the answer returns.
Accept the plan once the path reads cleanly, then add names after senior staff agree.
List every task before assigning any result, so no one is constrained by an early due line.
questions.explanation: The first need is the person, measure, and return. Listing every task overcorrects; it creates activity before anyone owes the result.

reviewCards.front: Why is a split not a result by itself?
reviewCards.back: AT&T separated Lucent Technologies in 1996, but the new shape still had to face capital-cycle pressure through due answers a business could read and correct.

reviewCards.front: What changes after the Honeywell-Alliedsignal close?
reviewCards.back: The close creates a combined industrial company. The advantage comes after that, when post-close habits make each promise visible enough to measure and fix.

reviewCards.front: What turns a clean promise into something usable?
reviewCards.back: It names the person, the due day, and the measured result. Without those three pieces, the sentence may sound good while no one can tell whether it delivered.

reviewCards.front: How is this different from micromanagement?
reviewCards.back: The senior person tests assumptions and removes barriers. They do not take over every task; the person doing the task still owns the act.

reviewCards.front: Why treat early bad news as useful?
reviewCards.back: Honest debate exposes weak assumptions while people, strategy, and operations can still adjust. Treating the signal as disloyal only hides the gap.

reviewCards.front: What should rewards teach?
reviewCards.back: Rewards should follow what came back, not the account that sounded best. People copy the behavior that receives credit.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a broad promise into a due answer. Ask for one person, one number, one day, and the business detail that could prove the promise thin. If the answer is blank, shrink the promise or set a lighter trial.

ifThenPlans.context: Measure one number when a handoff sounds settled.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the number has no person attached, then ask who owes the answer by the stated day before the handoff counts.

ifThenPlans.context: Measure one number when growth makes the path feel safe.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the number is only growth, then ask which assumption it tests and which barrier must move.

ifThenPlans.context: Measure one number when credit is being given.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the number tracks the account more than the result, then ask that credit follow what came back.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next status call, ask one active promise for 10 minutes: who owes which number by what day, and where will the answer be read?
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, observe one returned promise, then note one sentence: did the person, number, and due day change a decision or just fill a line?

memorableLines.text: The chart changes first; the business changes only when the number comes back.
A deadline is not a calendar square; it is the place where a promise answers.
Skipping the ask buys speed and pays it back as drift.

chapters.title: Building Block One: The Leader's Seven Essential Behaviors
chapters.hook: 7 promises looked signed until Ezra asked who would come back with proof.
chapters.counterintuition: Agreement nods; commitment signs. The surprise is that the seven behaviors are not traits to admire; they make each promise plain enough to inspect.
chapters.tryThisNow: Circle one live promise and write one number beside it: how many of the seven behaviors can be seen before the return pass?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use the seven behaviors as a short inspection list: tie each promise to a person, a visible measure, and a return pass before agreement counts.

breakdown.fastRead:
7 promises can look signed while no one can show who brings back proof. Ezra sees that in a first annual leadership assessment: each line has support, but the return point is blank.

The seven behaviors fix that false calm. Know the business close up. Insist on realism. Set clear priorities. Follow through. Reward doers. Grow people's judgment. Know yourself. Agreement nods; commitment signs. When a promise has a person, a visible measure, and a return pass, intention stops floating.
breakdown.deepRead:
Behavior makes a promise inspectable because it gives the promise a place to stand. A goal can sound clean in the room, yet stay vague unless someone asks who checks, what fact could change the answer, and when the return happens.

Jack Welch led General Electric from 1981 to 2001. The GE lesson here is not that a chief should collect reports from far away. It is that repeated passes made the business close enough for weak assumptions to be challenged before they hardened. Distance flatters. Close contact makes the miss harder to hide.

Ram Charan, a management adviser known for CEO and board counsel, brings the same pressure through questions. In client reviews, practical business talk forces a neat claim to face a person, a fact already in view, and a return point. The answer may feel slower. It is cleaner.

Ezra's first assessment fails because he rates tone instead of return. If he had treated the miss as a message problem, he would have improved the wording and left the same weak promise intact. The price of vague agreement is a second pass through the same fog.

Who checks, and when? That short question ties people, strategy, and operations without turning the job into a speech. A chief who welcomes early bad news can still be demanding. The demand is simply aimed at reality before the cost grows.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hard case is a smooth first assessment. Ezra and Dana can get every senior person to agree, yet still leave with weak work if the standard asks only whether the room felt aligned. That is why the checklist has to stay behavioral, not personal.

Use the Leader's Seven Essential Behaviors as questions, not slogans. Start with knowing the people and the business. Pair that with realism. Cut the goals to clear priorities. Bring promises back. Reward the doer. Grow judgment in others. Know yourself before bias bends the call. The list matters because each item asks for evidence in public view. Who knows the business well enough to challenge the claim? Which assumption is being protected from daylight? Which few goals deserve attention now? Which promise returns, and who is grown enough to judge without waiting for the top chair?

Larry Bossidy's case shows the reward side of the standard. The lesson is narrow and useful: priorities do not teach much until the pass and the reward system point at the same conduct. If the smooth speaker gets status while the doer brings proof alone, the culture has already learned the wrong rule.

This is also where the method costs something. Fewer priorities mean someone loses a favored project. Early bad news means a senior person may have to admit a bad read. Growing people means the top chair cannot stay the only source of judgment. Know yourself means bias is not a private flaw; it distorts staffing and operating calls. A fast close feels efficient. A false close is expensive.

Kendra's first version of the assessment tries to be fair by rating every promise gently. Ezra cuts it back. He asks which named person knows the business, which fact might prove the claim wrong, and which return point will expose a miss. Had they not done that, the broad agreement would have survived and the weak handoff would have moved forward under a clean title.

Do not use the seven behaviors as a way to punish every miss. A partial answer can be honest if it comes back early and names what is still unknown. The method fails when candor is treated as disloyalty, or when the checklist becomes a form that no one has to face again.

Make the promise answer back. That line keeps the work personal without making it a cult of personality. It is not about sounding tougher. It is about making the promise visible enough that the business can correct it while correction is still cheap.

examples.title: Yellow Pad Return
examples.scenario: Why did Ezra's annual pass hold this time? The answer sits on the yellow pad: Jack Welch at General Electric showed how repeated reviews kept the business close, so Ezra paid the cost in hours and returned to the weak line until a named person and visible fact were in view.
examples.whatToDo: Ezra turns the win into a question. He asks which person knew the business well enough to challenge the promise before it became a safer summary.
examples.whyItMatters: Ezra pays for close knowledge in time. Repeated passes keep a broad goal from hiding behind distance and rank.

examples.title: Outside The Reward Line
examples.scenario: Jenna arrives outside the operating review and hears the new rule from the customer partner: the next reward follows the person who brings proof back, not the cleanest promise. During Larry Bossidy's 1990s chief executive tenure, the pre-Honeywell merger operating improvement depended on reviews and rewards teaching which priorities counted. From outside the room, Jenna can tell whether the culture learned a rule or heard another speech.
examples.whatToDo: Jenna checks the reward trail after the review. Name the doer, the proof brought back, and the behavior the next team will copy.
examples.whyItMatters: An outside witness shows whether the system changed. If rewards still follow charm or rank, the stated priority has not reached the culture.

examples.title: Unmet Return Point
examples.scenario: Before the client names the miss, Dana sees one fact that will not sit straight. The target has a person, but the resource line does not match the promise. Ram Charan, the management adviser known for CEO and board counsel, would keep the practical question alive. Dana marks the cold coffee ring beside the gap. The return point is set; the answer is not yet met.
examples.whatToDo: Dana gives you the command: name the one fact that does not fit, assign the return point, and refuse to treat a neat answer as done.
examples.whyItMatters: Dana leaves you the warning: early bad news is data, not disloyalty. Use it before the hidden assumption gets costly.

examples.title: Standard Before Close
examples.scenario: The cost comes first as Ezra stops the annual leadership assessment from closing: no broad promise passes unless the seven behaviors make it observable. Jack Welch at General Electric is the benchmark for staying close, not praising the summary. Without that demand, good tone would hide weak responsibility. Kendra loses the easy close and has to return with the person, the fact, and the due return. The standard holds, and speed is the price.
examples.whatToDo: Ezra makes the cost visible: skipping this would let a broad promise pass. He slows the close until one person signs for the return.
examples.whyItMatters: Ezra's cost is the price of a real standard: skipping it buys speed while the same weak handoff survives under better wording.

questions.prompt: A clinic director hears clear agreement on a new discharge goal. Several actions could help. Which comes first, and why?
choices: Ask the senior physician to restate the goal for the clinic so staff know the message is official.
Tie the goal to a named person, visible proof, and a return pass so the promise can be corrected.
Freeze each discharge task until the clinic can write a full rule for every handoff and exception.
questions.explanation: The first move makes the promise inspectable. The physician restatement is tempting, but rank only gives the message a stronger source; it does not make the answer return.

questions.prompt: Your volunteer theater has many priorities before opening night. What maps best from the Bossidy lesson?
choices: Keep adding rehearsal goals until the cast sees how ambitious the production can become before opening night.
Link the top priorities to return passes and recognition, so cast members learn which acts carry weight.
Let the board chair choose the priority list, since the title alone will settle the theater's tradeoffs.
questions.explanation: The Bossidy pattern ties priorities to return and rewards. The chair option borrows rank, but it does not teach the cast which behavior earns weight.

questions.prompt: After a software team missed a launch, the director says the goal sounded strong. Which earlier failure best explains the miss?
choices: The director asked the communications group to rewrite the launch goal for the software team.
The director let the most senior architect approve the goal after the launch language felt persuasive.
The director relied on summary reports instead of repeated close passes through the business facts.
questions.explanation: The GE lesson favors direct, repeated contact with the business. Better wording tempts the director, but the miss came from distance, not weak phrasing.

questions.prompt: When a principal sees early bad news as disloyalty, her team stops raising staffing gaps. What is actually wrong?
choices: Her blind spot is bending people and operating calls before the hard signal can be used.
Her team needs a tighter calendar so each staffing gap gets an administrative due line.
Her deputy should filter the signals first, since rank can protect the principal's time.
questions.explanation: Self-knowledge matters because bias distorts people and operating calls. The calendar choice has a real tool, but it aims at timing while the blind spot remains.

questions.prompt: Several product leads leave a quarterly pass with warm agreement and fast growth. Which action belongs before they count it as done?
choices: Ask the growth lead to certify the pass, since scale shows the product group can carry the promise.
Bring each promise back to a stated return, so agreement becomes something the group sees again.
Wait until later results arrive, then decide whether the conversation mattered.
questions.explanation: Follow-through makes talk answer again. Growth can look persuasive, but scale does not prove the promise has a return point or a person who must bring it back.

questions.prompt: A city agency praised teamwork for months, yet employees copied the people who avoided hard delivery. Which earlier choice caused the drift?
choices: Status and resources went to the smooth talkers, so doers learned the agency's true standard.
The agency let a respected deputy explain teamwork, so staff waited for more official language.
The agency measured citizen demand more often, while the reward signal still pointed elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Rewards teach culture by showing which conduct wins status and support. Measuring demand may be useful, but it misses the agency's wrong reward signal.

questions.prompt: During a neighborhood festival, one coordinator answers every hard call and the helpers stay passive. What maps from capability building?
choices: Let helpers make smaller judgment calls with feedback, so the coordinator is no longer the only brain in the system.
Hand every hard call to helpers at once, so the coordinator proves trust and stops being the bottleneck.
Set firmer event deadlines for helpers, since the calendar is the main device for accountability.
questions.explanation: Capability grows when judgment spreads beyond one person. The handoff-everything option over-corrects; it removes the bottleneck by dumping judgment too fast.

questions.prompt: A warehouse supervisor gets neat updates, but the first bad signal arrives late and costs more. What is the deeper fault?
choices: The supervisor let the shift lead rank the updates, trusting role status to sort the real signal.
The supervisor pushed for more confident personalities, hoping stronger voices would make delays visible sooner.
The supervisor made bad signals feel risky, so hidden assumptions stayed hidden until they were expensive.
questions.explanation: Realism asks for bad signals early. The stronger-personality fix is tempting, but it treats candor as style instead of changing what happens to bad news.

questions.prompt: Suppose a grant committee leaves a planning call with many attractive goals. What should come first before anyone accepts the list?
choices: Cut every goal that lacks an immediate funding win, even before the committee sees the tradeoff.
Let the largest donor choose the list, since outside rank will help the committee focus more quickly.
Name the few priorities that deserve attention, so the committee does not spread effort too thin.
questions.explanation: Clear priorities protect attention and responsibility. The donor option borrows authority, but focus has to come from choosing the few goals the group can truly carry.

reviewCards.front: What are the seven behaviors a senior person uses to make a promise inspectable?
reviewCards.back: Start with Know your people and your business. Add Insist on realism and Set clear goals and priorities. Then Follow through, Reward the doers, Expand people's capabilities, and Know yourself.

reviewCards.front: What does Jack Welch at General Electric teach about knowing the business?
reviewCards.back: Under Jack Welch, General Electric made close knowledge a repeated pass through the business, not distant reporting. The senior person stays near enough to challenge weak assumptions.

reviewCards.front: How did the Bossidy case connect priorities with consequences?
reviewCards.back: Larry Bossidy's case ties priorities to operating passes and rewards. People learned the standard from what came back and what earned status.

reviewCards.front: Why should bad news arrive early?
reviewCards.back: Early bad news lets a leader use the signal while correction is still cheaper. Hidden assumptions get expensive when people learn to protect comfort instead of reality.

reviewCards.front: What changes when follow-through is real?
reviewCards.back: A conversation becomes execution only when the promise is checked again. The return point shows whether the named person brought back the fact the group needed.

reviewCards.front: How do self-knowledge and capability building protect judgment?
reviewCards.back: Self-knowledge keeps blind spots from bending people and operating calls. Capability building spreads judgment so the top chair is not the only source of decisions.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning agreement into something visible. Use Make the Promise Answer Back by naming who signs, what hard fact returns, and which of the seven behaviors is missing. The skill is not a bigger speech; it is a short pass that can catch weak reality early.

ifThenPlans.context: A promise leaves a call with broad agreement.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a promise leaves a call with broad agreement, then run Make the Promise Answer Back: write who signs for it and what fact returns.

ifThenPlans.context: Bad news arrives before the scheduled return.
ifThenPlans.plan: If bad news arrives before the scheduled return, then ask who checks, and when, then move the return closer.

ifThenPlans.context: A person gets praised for smooth talk.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a person gets praised for smooth talk, then run Make the Promise Answer Back by asking what doer earned status and what proof came back.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Replace one status email today with a circled promise: named person, visible fact, and return time. Send that version before the day ends.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Before a weekly meeting you already attend, choose a live promise, circle the missing behavior, and move one return point closer.

memorableLines.text: The price of vague agreement is a second pass through the same fog.
Who checks, and when?

chapters.title: Building Block Two: Creating the Framework for Cultural Change
chapters.hook: What makes a culture claim survive the first missed promise instead of becoming a poster?
chapters.counterintuition: You may expect culture to change when the words get clearer. The harder truth is that it changes when a visible act is tied to a person, a measure, and a return pass.
chapters.tryThisNow: Schedule a 15-minute return pass for one promise; write the behavior and line that will prove it happened.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat culture as an operating ledger: a stated behavior, a named person, a visible line, and a return pass tied to reward or consequence.

breakdown.fastRead:
What makes that claim survive at Honeywell after 1999? Honeywell is a large industrial company, and its modern form includes a 1999 integration. The case matters because a merged business can say one culture and still let old local habits keep running.

The move is plain. Say the behavior that must be seen. Put a person and a line beside it. Bring it back soon enough for reward or consequence to teach the standard. A poster can express a hope; an operating routine makes the hope answer back. Culture does not start in the speech; it shows up after the miss.
breakdown.deepRead:
Clemence and Henry disagree about the annual leadership assessment before anyone fills in a score. "If the language is clear, people will know what we mean," Henry says. Clemence answers, "They will know what we value when they see what comes back." The split matters. If reward and consequence point away from the stated behavior, the older rule wins.

This is why GE Crotonville belongs here. GE Crotonville is the leadership center that opened in 1956 for leadership development. Its lesson is not a campus story; it is that common management language can be built on purpose. People learn which words matter when the same words keep meeting real business lines, not when a staff group files a better phrase.

Candid dialogue is the hinge. It lets weak assumptions get spoken while they are still cheap to change. You do not ask for candor so everyone feels free. You ask for it because people, strategy, and operations touch each other, and one hidden assumption can spoil all three.

The Home Depot gives the frontline edge. The Home Depot was founded in 1978, and its retail operating model linked store behavior with customer service. In a store, "be helpful" is too soft. Did the habit show up for the customer, and did the store result move in the right direction? No visible line, no learning.

Make the miss teach. That is the short command. A return line is not admin; it is how the promise learns. Once the behavior returns, the group can praise what matched the standard, face what missed, and change the load before the same miss repeats.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hard case is not open resistance. The hard case is a smooth yes. After the 1999 Honeywell integration, a team could agree with the new standard and still keep the old local habit if no one had to show the act again. Agreement feels cheap. The miss is where price appears.

Build the ledger in this order. First, name the behavior a bystander could see or hear. Second, put one person near the line that will tell the truth. Third, set the return pass close enough that the answer can still be changed. Fourth, make reward or consequence match the result. That sequence turns a value into business evidence without pretending a speech changed the company.

What if the line looks bad? Good. Early bad news is not disloyal; it is the first usable signal. Performance culture fails when effort gets praised while missed promises carry no consequence. People learn that the safe act is trying hard in public and missing quietly later. That is not discipline. It is drift with applause.

The same idea explains why Crotonville matters. GE Crotonville opened in 1956 for leadership development, so its lesson is not a lone campus fact. Shared language is built when phrases are tested against the same business questions again and again. If "customer focus" means one thing in a leadership session and another thing in a store aisle, the words have not been built. They have only been repeated.

Home Depot adds the store view. The Home Depot was founded in 1978, and its retail operating model makes the lesson concrete. A frontline habit has to touch a customer or store result. If the habit improves neither, it may be pleasant, but it is not part of performance culture. You can praise energy and still train the wrong act. If reward and stated value split, reward wins.

This is also why communications staff cannot install culture for you. They can help words travel. They cannot decide which miss gets faced, which act gets rewarded, or which early signal stops a bad claim. Those are repeated choices by the people with authority over staffing, strategy, and operations.

Use deadlines with care. A deadline is a promise with a return point, not a calendar mark. Treat it as an accountability device: a way to know when the promise must face the ledger. Without that return, the deadline becomes admin noise, and everyone learns to wait for the next push.

The move has limits. Do not use it to turn every small trial into a burden. Some exploratory work should stay loose until there is enough evidence to judge it. Do not punish honest bad news, or the ledger will go dark. Do the opposite when learning is still the main task: widen the search, protect candor, and delay consequence until the standard is fair. The cost is real. This method spends time, status, and comfort. Use it when the behavior is central enough that a miss should teach the business before the same miss repeats.

examples.title: Integration Standard At Risk
examples.scenario: Name the integration standard before the sign-offs move: culture must show up as a behavior tied to a person and a visible line. Honeywell's 1999 integration gives the setting, because a large industrial portfolio could keep old habits unless the new standard returned. The first pass is headed for a miss. A late return catches one local habit barely before it becomes the new normal.
examples.whatToDo: The standard line shows the danger. Schedule the return before the promise leaves, name the person, and write the measure that will expose a miss.
examples.whyItMatters: The late ledger tells you why. Do not count agreement as culture; count the behavior that comes back with reward or consequence attached.

examples.title: Unpaid Language
examples.scenario: The cost shows up before the wording is settled: Henry is already crossing out a term when Maxwell stops him. "We used the same word, but not the same act," Maxwell says. GE Crotonville, opened in 1956 for leadership development, is the benchmark: shared management language has to be built, then brought back. The next leadership session carries the return pass, and it has not happened yet.
examples.whatToDo: The skipped return shows what the group pays: common words lose bite. Henry sets one pass where each term must meet a real choice.
examples.whyItMatters: The open line shows the unpaid bill: words can sound shared while choices stay separate. The return point keeps the language from drifting.

examples.title: Store Line Earned
examples.scenario: The mechanism shows up at the return pass: Violette reads the same store result twice. Before the reset, a service habit was praised while the customer result stayed weak. Once reset, the habit is tied to the store outcome, and the missed promise carries a consequence. The Home Depot was founded in 1978; its retail operating model gives the test: frontline conduct has to reach the customer.
examples.whatToDo: The mechanism explains why it works: the habit is no longer separate from the customer result. Violette matches praise to the outcome.
examples.whyItMatters: The store ledger pays the cost: effort praise alone loses cover. When consequence matches the stated habit, the old rule weakens.

examples.title: Late Trace
examples.scenario: Why is a red mark still sitting on the Honeywell ledger? Because the standard named a behavior, but the return sat too far away. The 1999 integration catches the local habit, barely, when the line finally forces a person to face the miss. The team is looking back from the edge, not celebrating a clean pass.
examples.whatToDo: The red mark asks the question: why so late? Answer by moving the return closer and naming which local habit must change before the next pass.
examples.whyItMatters: The red mark gives the answer: a standard without a timely return lets old habits run. Late is better than never; earlier is cheaper.

examples.title: Customer Pays
examples.scenario: A customer reaches Maxwell first: service sounded busy, but the outcome did not move. The Home Depot was founded in 1978, and its retail operating model makes the failure plain: praise effort while the customer result stays weak, and the model learns the wrong act. The move was skipped; the miss lands outside the group that made the promise.
examples.whatToDo: Fix the failure. Tie praise to the customer outcome, and make the missed promise carry a consequence before effort becomes the standard.
examples.whyItMatters: Praise without consequence teaches effort, not service. The buyer feels the miss.

examples.title: Early Signal On The Board
examples.scenario: Catch the phrase while the room still thinks it agrees: the same words are being used two ways. GE Crotonville is the leadership development case where shared language is built through repeated management dialogue. Chalk dust hangs over the board. Clemence stops the session, sets the return pass, and pays the cost of slowing a group that wanted to move on; the term comes back with one meaning.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the shared word, write the behavior it must mean, and schedule the return pass before it spreads.
examples.whyItMatters: The board shows the price. Slow the group now; otherwise the same word will hide different choices and the center will teach noise.

questions.prompt: A department says it values ownership, but no one can point to the behavior due this week. What is actually wrong?
choices: The due line is enough evidence, so the group should wait to see whether belief strengthens under pressure.
The belief is too vague; it needs an observable act, a person near it, and a return line.
The group should define more values for every role, even if no single act is brought back soon.
questions.explanation: The trouble is vagueness. A due line can help, but timing matters only when a visible act and person come back to face it.

questions.prompt: Several store leads praise effort after a missed customer promise and avoid consequence. What happens downstream?
choices: The miss can wait until the next cycle, since public thanks keeps people willing to try again.
The effort praise proves the culture is healthy, so the group can treat the miss as a one-off gap.
The old rule gets taught: trying hard receives credit while the unmet promise carries no real cost.
questions.explanation: Praise teaches only when the miss has a cost. The later-cycle answer sounds humane, but it delays the signal and tells people effort is enough.

questions.prompt: At a leadership center, shared terms sound settled but choices still diverge. What should happen next?
choices: Build the common language through repeated leader dialogue tied to choices, measures, and a return pass.
Let training staff own the language now that the broad goal is persuasive enough to repeat.
Write a glossary for every group, then check adoption after the terms have spread across the business for a full cycle.
questions.explanation: Shared language is built through repeated leader development, not handed off after the goal sounds good. A glossary starts the move but stops before choices test it.

questions.prompt: During rapid growth, the weekly forum repeats numbers but never teaches which ones matter. Which principle is violated?
choices: Growth itself has settled the issue, so the forum can stay broad while the business keeps scaling.
The forum should collect more numbers, then sort them after people have already acted on the broad claim.
The repeated forum must train attention on the few visible lines that guide choices and return later.
questions.explanation: The forum has to train attention. Growth is tempting proof, but scale can hide a weak discipline unless repeated passes teach which lines matter.

questions.prompt: Honeywell teams agree on integration language, yet local habits keep running. What is the single best move?
choices: Turn the integration claim into one visible act with a named person, a measure, and a near return pass.
Send a clearer culture memo so each site hears the same words before judging which habits changed.
Wait until the full integration settles, then compare which local habits survived across sites and write the lessons for later.
questions.explanation: Honeywell's integration lesson is mechanism, not wording. The clearer memo travels farther, but it still lets local habits survive without a visible return.

questions.prompt: A store habit feels energetic but customer and store results do not move. What is missing?
choices: More ambition is missing, so the store should raise the service target before asking for proof.
The habit has not been tied to the customer result and store outcome it is meant to change in practice.
The store should praise the habit first, then look for customer effects after the team feels the behavior is normal.
questions.explanation: Home Depot's store case ties habit to customer and store results. Raising ambition sounds useful, yet it skips the proof that the habit changes outcomes.

questions.prompt: Suppose rewards still favor the old behavior while the new standard is repeated. What follows?
choices: The group should study personalities first, because resistant people are the main reason the standard stalls.
The old behavior keeps its pull because reward and consequence still do not match the stated standard in daily choices.
The repeated standard will win once people have heard it enough times and can recite the desired behavior under pressure.
questions.explanation: Reward is the teacher here. Hearing the standard more often may help memory, but it cannot beat a system that keeps paying the old behavior.

questions.prompt: The communications group is asked to install the new culture after senior choices stay unchanged. Which principle breaks?
choices: Culture is being handed to message carriers, while the choices that reward behavior stay untouched.
The staff group is too narrow; every support function should share the wording before choices change.
Senior people are choosing too soon; they should wait until the message has traveled before changing rewards.
questions.explanation: Communications can carry words, not install choices. Wider wording is a tempting scope fix, but reward and consequence still have to change.

questions.prompt: A quarterly pass looks clean, but conflict and weak assumptions never surface. What did the group mistake for proof?
choices: They raised hard questions too early, before the group had enough time to show the promise could hold.
They gathered visible lines and named people, then stopped before anyone had to discuss the weak assumption out loud.
They treated a clean exchange as delivery proof even though candor had not tested the risky parts in public.
questions.explanation: Candor makes weak assumptions discussable. The named-lines answer has useful parts, but it stops before conflict tests the risk, so the clean pass is false comfort.

reviewCards.front: Why did Honeywell's 1999 integration need more than shared language?
reviewCards.back: Old habits can survive a merger unless the new behavior is tied to a person, visible line, and return pass. That is why the integration case teaches operating practice, not poster language.

reviewCards.front: What does GE Crotonville show about shared management language?
reviewCards.back: The center opened in 1956 for leadership development. Its lesson here is that shared language can be built on purpose when words keep returning to real business choices.

reviewCards.front: What does The Home Depot add to the culture lesson?
reviewCards.back: Founded in 1978, The Home Depot grounds the lesson in store behavior. A frontline habit matters when it connects to customer and store outcomes.

reviewCards.front: Why must rewards and consequences match the new standard?
reviewCards.back: People copy what the system pays for. If praise or consequence points to the old behavior, the stated value loses to the actual signal.

reviewCards.front: Why is candid dialogue part of culture change?
reviewCards.back: It makes conflict and weak assumptions discussable while they can still be changed. A clean pass without candor may hide the risk that matters most.

reviewCards.front: Why are observable behaviors stricter than beliefs?
reviewCards.back: Beliefs are too vague to manage by themselves. Observable behavior can be named, brought back, and tied to a result, so missed promises carry real weight.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use a small ledger for one behavior you want to change. Write the visible act, the person closest to it, the line that will tell the truth, and the return pass. Then match praise or consequence to what comes back. The tool is small because the point is not a perfect values statement; the point is a promise the business can inspect.

ifThenPlans.context: When you observe a value stated as a belief, note the behavior a bystander would see.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the behavior is not visible, then rewrite the promise as one act with one return pass.

ifThenPlans.context: When you observe early bad news treated as disloyal, note the missed signal it is trying to surface.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the signal is punished, then reset the pass so bad news is treated as data before judgment.

ifThenPlans.context: When you observe praise after a missed promise, note whether consequence matched the standard.
ifThenPlans.plan: If praise covers the miss, then name the cost and move reward back to the behavior that returned with proof.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Schedule a 15-minute return pass by sending this exact sentence: "Let's schedule 15 minutes tomorrow to name who will show the behavior and what line will tell us."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, run a two-step sequence: first, schedule a 30-minute ledger pass for one stated behavior; second, close it by recording the result, reward or consequence, and the next return pass.

Culture does not start in the speech; it shows up after the miss.
