chapters.title: Building Block Three: The Job No Leader Should Delegate: Having the Right People in the Right Place
chapters.hook: Eliana pauses at the last name and asks what this role will demand first.
chapters.counterintuition: The staffing call is not cleanup after strategy. It is where the strategy first becomes either believable or soft.
chapters.tryThisNow: When a key role gets a favorite name, read aloud one sentence: this role will strain at __, and we have seen __ handle that strain.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not hand away the people call. Match each hard role to seen behavior and judgment before the goal becomes a promise others have to carry.

breakdown.fastRead:
Eliana pauses at the last name and asks what this role will demand first. A familiar name is on top. She does not ask who is owed a bigger title. She asks who has already shown the judgment the job will need.

GE Session C (General Electric's structured annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure) is the case. It made role fit a repeated senior duty, not a yearly HR file. Role fit means matching the job's demand with behavior a person has already shown.

That is the job a senior person should not hand away. A goal is only as strong as the person placed under it. Talent is behavior against demand, not a grand title.
breakdown.deepRead:
The move works because a named person makes a promise testable. If Eliana writes the service demand beside Yvonne's name, the group can ask what evidence supports it and when the gap will come back. A broad goal cannot answer those questions.

Use the full pass only for senior, costly, or reset-linked choices. For a small and easy-to-reverse assignment, use the light version: say the demand, name the person, and decide what would prove the fit wrong. The full version fails when it becomes a slow court case or a sponsor's way to protect a favorite. Then choose the smaller screen and keep moving.

IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition (IBM naming Lou Gerstner chief executive as the company moved from a hardware-centered identity toward services and integrated solutions) shows the stakes. A reset does not only need new language. It needs people who can lead the new task when old habits pull back.

Who has shown the judgment this new demand will need? That question keeps the title from doing the thinking. Eliana asks it before the name goes final, because resume strength can open the conversation but cannot close it.

Succession belongs here too. A future handoff is not an admin chore. It is a promise made early. The name written now should match behavior already seen, and the follow-up should say what gap must change before the handoff is real.
breakdown.fullRead:
Reagan starts from a different end: an executive choice that already carries a business bet. The Home Depot's 2000 Nardelli appointment (the company hired Robert Nardelli as chief executive after his GE career for a scaling retail challenge) shows that a hire imports assumptions, not just skill.

The lesson is not that outsiders solve scale, or that insiders should be preferred. The lesson is to say what the hire is supposed to prove. A GE career may signal operating discipline; in The Home Depot case, the match still had to be argued against the retail challenge in front of the company.

A weak people call makes a strong strategy pay for the gap. People watch the selection and learn what seems to count. If the imported pattern fits the need, the signal helps. If the pattern is trusted because of rank or brand, the gap moves into daily operations.

GE Session C adds the repeat. Its annual talent reviews mattered when senior people returned to role fit and named performance gaps. Praise that never changes a choice is not candor. It is cover.

Maverick states the standard this way: do not reward language you cannot connect to behavior. If a person is praised as ready but no one can name a judgment already shown, the word is too light. Development or replacement should stay available while the gap can still be faced.

IBM gives the reset version. In 1993, IBM put Lou Gerstner in the top role during a shift beyond its old hardware center into services plus integrated solutions. Had the reset been handed to people matched only to the old identity, the language could have changed faster than the capability underneath it. That is a way to reason about your own case, not a hidden claim about IBM's details.

The light version matters here. Do not run a full talent argument for every short task. When the choice is low risk and easy to undo, write the demand, put a person beside it, and state the sign that would show a mismatch. Use the heavy version when the role is senior, costly, or tied to a reset. A light screen still has teeth if a named person, a seen behavior, and a follow-up point are written where the group will read them. What it drops is ceremony, not judgment.

What does this role assume about the business? Ask that before you ask who has the best record. The resume can start the file. It cannot make the promise true. The senior duty is to keep the role, the seen behavior, and the follow-up point in one line where the group can read it.

examples.title: Session C After Praise
examples.scenario: GE Session C is over, and Eliana has one problem still open. The mechanism has to turn praise into a role-fit claim before the weak choice hardens. General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure did not fail because people were quiet; they failed when praise covered a role gap. A blue pencil mark sits under ready. The follow-up point is set, but no one has yet shown the behavior the harder role needs.
examples.whatToDo: Skip this and the praise becomes the proof. Eliana should turn ready into a short claim: what the role demands, what behavior has been seen, and what gap must come back.
examples.whyItMatters: Leave the gap unnamed and development stays vague. The Session C duty works because the same name returns with evidence, not because the file looks neat.

examples.title: Yvonne Feels The Reset
examples.scenario: What changes when Lou Gerstner arrives from outside IBM in 1993? Yvonne sees the answer as one reset assignment moves from broad language to a person with matched judgment. As IBM moves from hardware identity toward services and integrated solutions, old status loses cover. The clean win is not the slogan; it is the new demand, the person, and the observed judgment fitting before the assignment hardens.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the match and staff inherit a slogan. Yvonne should hold the assignment open until the new demand, the person, and observed judgment fit.
examples.whyItMatters: Let rank settle it and the reset gets cheaper at first, then weaker under strain. The cost paid is familiar status losing cover.

examples.title: The Career Signal
examples.scenario: Before anyone names it, Reagan sees the GE career becoming the answer. The Home Depot's 2000 Nardelli appointment, a chief executive hired after a GE career for a scaling retail challenge, carried an operating assumption. The folder corner is bent. Name the assumption now, and the strong resume does not pass for fit until the miss is hard to move.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the assumption and ambition fills the gap. Reagan should name what the hire is supposed to prove before the career record settles the call.
examples.whyItMatters: Borrowed status travels fast. Context decides late, when the selection has already told people which habits seem to count.

examples.title: Maverick Tests The Gap
examples.scenario: Start with the role demand: the candidate has not shown the missing behavior yet. Maverick, keep GE Session C praise from closing the file inside General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure. The named gap creates only a partial win until the team chooses development against that behavior or replacement for the role. If the compliment settles it, candor has only delayed the same weak fit.
examples.whatToDo: Make the fork explicit. Either assign development against the named behavior and bring it back, or replace for the role demand.
examples.whyItMatters: A people process earns its force at this point. Vague approval blocks both growth and replacement; a named choice turns the gap into execution work.

examples.title: Eliana Audits The Assignment
examples.scenario: The cost shows up while Eliana is auditing the IBM reset roster: one assignment has a name beside it, but no observed judgment for the new work. After Lou Gerstner's 1993 arrival, the company is moving from a hardware-centered identity toward services and integrated solutions. The margin note stays blank until the team names evidence or reassigns the work. The clean win is a roster that proves capability before the handoff hardens.
examples.whatToDo: Mark any assignment that lacks seen judgment for the new task. Keep it open until evidence appears, or reassign it to someone whose behavior fits the work.
examples.whyItMatters: Agreement can masquerade as fit when the roster looks complete. The audit protects the reset by making capability visible before the handoff hardens.

questions.prompt: A hospital launches a new access model. The staffing group keeps early complaints out of the operations talk because they sound negative. Which principle does that break?
choices: Staffing signals belong beside the operating choices, since those calls set how much the access model can actually carry.
Staffing can be tuned after launch, since complaints become clearer once the access model meets real volume.
The most senior clinicians should own the access model, since authority keeps early complaints from slowing the change or raising doubts.
questions.explanation: Early complaints are useful evidence about the staffing ceiling. The launch-first choice sounds disciplined, but it waits until the limit has already formed.

questions.prompt: When a theater hires a director from a strong resume but has no evidence under strain, what should be asked first?
choices: Use the resume as a starting proof, then watch the first hard season for signs of judgment before changes are made.
Ask which past choice proves the candidate can use sound judgment when the job's hard part arrives in practice.
Delay the hire until every stakeholder agrees there is no remaining risk in the choice or its timing.
questions.explanation: The right screen looks for behavior and judgment before the choice closes. The delay answer values caution, but it replaces judgment with a search for certainty.

questions.prompt: Before a grant team accepts a bold delivery promise, it asks HR to rank candidates for the hardest post. What comes first?
choices: Let HR rank the candidates first; the project lead can step in later if delivery starts to slip badly.
Pick the person with the best style for the team, then adjust the promise around that person's strengths and history.
Keep the capability call with the promise holder, while HR helps collect evidence for that final decision.
questions.explanation: The person accepting the promise has to keep the capability judgment. The HR-first option gathers help, but gives away the call until slippage appears.

questions.prompt: Your neighborhood co-op needs a future treasurer before the current one leaves. Which choice maps best?
choices: Wait for the vacancy, then choose whoever handles the first urgent finance task with the least friction and fewest questions.
Ask the current treasurer for a trusted helper and use tenure to settle any close choice.
Prepare someone before the handoff, because future promises depend on judgment already seen in the role.
questions.explanation: Succession is part of delivery because later promises need prepared judgment. The tenure answer feels orderly, but it uses closeness instead of proved fit.

questions.prompt: A museum board recruits an operator with a famous career to manage growth. What should it examine before treating the hire as fit?
choices: Ask what operating assumption the hire brings, then compare that assumption with the museum's growth problem.
Use the famous career to get the hire started, then compare assumptions once growth pressure is visible to the staff.
Measure whether internal candidates feel slighted, then treat that reaction as the main fit signal.
questions.explanation: The selection carries a business bet, so the bet has to match the real growth problem. The quick-start answer borrows trust from career strength.

questions.prompt: Even with full enrollment, a training program gives its hardest cohort to someone with weak judgment. Why is growth not enough?
choices: Scale can hide weak fit; the promise stays fragile when the named person cannot carry the hardest demand.
Scale gives the person more chances to learn, so the gap should wait until demand settles.
A wider support circle can absorb the strain, so the assignment can stay unchanged while help increases over time.
questions.explanation: Growth can mask a poor match, but it does not create the capability the hard post needs. The support answer treats help as a substitute for fit.

questions.prompt: During a library talent discussion before branch assignments renew, a struggling candidate gets broad praise but no named gap. Which fix follows?
choices: Keep the praise and wait for patron strain before naming the gap in a later staffing talk with more evidence from patrons.
Name the gap while choices remain open, so development or replacement can still follow before the role hardens.
Separate praise from role decisions, so the candidate hears support before any hard choice is made.
questions.explanation: Candor matters when it lets a development or replacement choice happen. Waiting for patron strain lets praise keep hiding the gap until the role is harder to move.

questions.prompt: After a city agency agrees on a service reset for a public benefits office, staff want broad goals first and people sorted later. Why is that risky?
choices: Let staff translate the reset after support functions understand the new direction and report back with early lessons.
Protect the familiar posts until the reset has proved demand across the agency and the old habits are stable.
Match people to the new demand before the goal is handed down, or the reset can sound clear and stay loose under strain.
questions.explanation: A reset needs people able to lead the new task, not only a shared goal. The staff-translation answer moves the words along while delaying the match.

questions.prompt: Suppose a youth nonprofit copies an annual talent form from a large company before assigning camp directors. What is missing from the copy?
choices: A cleaner yearly cycle, with each role scored once and stored for the staff file before camp starts.
A repeated fit conversation that keeps fresh evidence beside hard roles after the form is filled.
A chief executive instinct call that can override the cycle whenever familiar names feel safer.
questions.explanation: GE Session C teaches recurrence, not storage. The cleaner-cycle answer looks organized, but it turns a senior duty into a file instead of a live fit call.

reviewCards.front: What people call should stay with the senior person?
reviewCards.back: The senior person keeps the link between role demand and capability. Others can collect evidence, but the final judgment cannot be handed off.

reviewCards.front: What does GE Session C add to the lesson?
reviewCards.back: It makes role fit recurring. General Electric's annual talent reviews during Jack Welch's tenure matter here because the duty comes back instead of ending as HR paperwork.

reviewCards.front: Why does the IBM transition belong in a staffing chapter?
reviewCards.back: IBM's 1993 Gerstner transition moved from hardware identity toward services and integrated solutions. The reset needed people able to lead the new task.

reviewCards.front: What question does The Home Depot case raise?
reviewCards.back: Ask what operating assumption comes with the hire. The 2000 Nardelli appointment after a GE career shows that selection carries a business bet.

reviewCards.front: Why can vague praise harm a staffing choice?
reviewCards.back: It hides the gap that should guide development or replacement. Warm language helps only when it does not block the hard choice.

reviewCards.front: Why is succession part of this same duty?
reviewCards.back: Future promises depend on prepared people. A likely handoff should match someone whose judgment has been seen before the role changes hands.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Pick one hard role. Read aloud the demand, the person, and the behavior already seen under strain. If the sentence cannot name behavior, keep the choice open or use the light version for a small reversible call.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: This role will strain first at __.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the answer is only a resume, then ask for behavior already seen under that strain.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: Praise has not settled the choice.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the gap is unnamed, then name it before deciding on development or replacement.

ifThenPlans.context: Say aloud: This reset still needs a person who can carry it.
ifThenPlans.plan: If no one has shown judgment for the new demand, then keep the assignment open while evidence is gathered.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Spend 20 minutes reading aloud one live role sentence until it names the strain, the person, and the behavior already seen.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, observe one planned handoff; then note the demand, the named person, and one behavior that supports or weakens the match.

chapters.title: The People Process: Making the Link with Strategy and Operations
chapters.hook: The best people process starts by mistrusting a strong score.
chapters.counterintuition: You may think a high rating settles the talent question. It does not. A hard promise needs a named person, clear proof, and a return point.
chapters.tryThisNow: Cross-out names on one live talent list for 10 minutes: strike each name with no proof for the role, then write the first missing proof in plain words.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A people process is real only when it changes the staffing path: pair the score with the backup line, name proof, and return before the budget trusts it.

breakdown.fastRead:
A good score can be the weakest sign in a people process. That feels wrong. But a score looks back. A hard choice and a budget look ahead.

Tanner sees that in GE's annual talent review, the leadership-assessment pass tied to succession planning. The old question is, did this person do well? The sharper question is, who can carry the role if the load rises or the seat opens?

So the GE talent pass has to read past results with the backup line. It asks for a named person, plain proof, and a return point. Agreement nods; commitment signs. When those pieces are missing, the answer is not a better speech. It is coaching, a role shift, a new choice, or a smaller aim.
breakdown.deepRead:
The link works only when the talent talk changes a real choice. If the output is a neat score, you still have a wish. Who checks the bench before the budget trusts it?

Inside GE's succession-linked talent review, Tanner is not asking for a kinder label. He is asking whether the person in the role has enough bench behind the role. A strong record can be true and still leave the business thin. Past results and the backup line have to be read together, or the budget will count strength that is not there. Names are not enough.

Honeywell, an industrial company with a broad portfolio after a 1999 merger, makes that gap easier to see. Aerospace, automation, and materials do not call for the same bench. One list can look full while one unit has the wrong depth. The broad goal may sound clear. The work will still ask, who is ready for this load?

This is where people, strategy, and operations meet. If a choice needs a lead the company has not made ready, the choice is not ready. If a budget assumes a team can carry more than it can, the numbers have borrowed from a blank space. A title is not proof.

The limit matters. Do not turn every score talk into a trial. Some roles are steady, and a plain appraisal may be enough. But when the load grows, or when a missing backup changes the risk, soft praise costs more than candor. The least welcome line may be the most useful one: the bench is not ready.
breakdown.fullRead:
Paige's partial miss shows where the move breaks. The score looked strong. The backup answer stayed thin. By the time the gap was named, the budget had already assumed strength. The people pass did not fail for lack of drive. It failed because praise beat proof.

At GE's annual talent pass, the answer has to do more than sort people into high and low rows. It has to change what happens now. One person may need coaching. Another may need a different role. A third may have to be replaced. The key point is blunt: if no path changes, the talent talk has not done its job.

This is also why a clear talk is not enough. A better memo can say that the team values depth, but the unit still needs a name, proof, and a point where the answer comes back. Who checks, and when? Without that return, a weak answer can hide under a strong score for another cycle.

Honeywell widens the lens. After the 1999 merger, Honeywell's industrial portfolio covered materials, aerospace, and automation. That mix makes one master bench too neat. The person who fits one business may not fit another. A thin spot in one unit can make a clean growth choice false. Talent sets the promise; the promise does not set talent.

Procter & Gamble, founded in 1837 and known for an internal leadership pipeline, shows the long side. A promote-from-within system cannot be made at the moment a new choice needs it. It has to spot high-potential people early, give them real prep, and make backup strength visible before the future depends on it. Slow prep buys speed later.

The hard part is candor. If the people pass becomes a hunt for flaws, staff will hide the first bad signal. If each gap means a firing case, no one will bring the early news that could save the choice. Paige's miss carries the boundary: use the proof to change a path, not to shame the person who brought the proof.

Candid calibration means ratings are made useful. It does not mean cruel talk. Inflated scores hide risk in the plan. Clear scores show where to coach, move, replace, or wait. Do not let praise outrun proof.

Ask what the talent call produced. Did someone get training tied to the gap? Did a role move? Did a weak seat get a new choice? Did the backup line become clear? If the answer is only a score, the business has not earned trust in the promise. People do not serve strategy after the budget is set. They decide what the strategy can honestly promise.

examples.title: Tanner Halts The Rating
examples.scenario: GE talent lead Tanner states the demand during annual leadership assessment before a high score can close: no rating passes with a blank backup answer. GE's talent review tied to succession planning has to protect the unit that will feel a weak handoff. Tanner slows the close, cuts the easy praise, and makes the score face the seat risk.
examples.whatToDo: Who can carry it? Pair the score with the backup answer before the rating passes, even when the high mark feels earned. Make the promise name proof.
examples.whyItMatters: What changes? The score stops acting like proof by itself. The business pays the short cost before a weak handoff gets dear.

examples.title: Ella Splits The Bench
examples.scenario: Operations lead Ella's red pen stops on aerospace. The post-1999 depth demand has already been set. Honeywell, an industrial company with a broad portfolio after a 1999 merger, cannot treat aerospace, automation, and materials as one bench. The slate is headed for a miss until she ties each promise to the person ready for that business. The save comes late.
examples.whatToDo: Which business is harder than the list admits? Split the call by aerospace, automation, and materials; name depth for each before the broad goal moves.
examples.whyItMatters: Why push now? Make the broad goal face the true load before staff inherits a promise one list cannot carry across unlike businesses.

examples.title: Stuart Keeps The Return Open
examples.scenario: Stuart starts at the return point, not at launch. Procter & Gamble, founded in 1837 and known for its internal leadership pipeline, has taught him that promotion from within is strong only when prep is visible. His business aim stays open: a high-potential person has a path to grow, but the backup answer is not met yet.
examples.whatToDo: What does skipping cost? Ambition borrows from people not yet ready. Set a return point and leave the choice open until backup proof comes back.
examples.whyItMatters: Which risk remains? The long pipeline helps only if the business waits for proof; a proud heritage cannot carry a future role by itself.

examples.title: Paige Traces The Split
examples.scenario: Facilitator Paige starts after the miss in GE's annual leadership assessment follow-up. The rating said ready; the backup answer said thin. The open folder stayed between them. Tracing GE's review tied to succession planning, she finds the split: the score had passed without a candid backup call. The fix works, but it costs status; the high rating is cut back before the staffing path is trusted.
examples.whatToDo: Why does the trace work? It joins the score to backup risk, then cuts the rating back before the budget treats strength as settled.
examples.whyItMatters: How is the cost earned? Inflated ratings protect comfort; candid calibration protects the business from a promise its people cannot meet.

questions.prompt: Your youth robotics club gives every mentor a strong annual score while the new season asks for harder build commitments. What is wrong with using the scores alone?
choices: Ask the head coach to certify the scores this week, since a respected title will settle which mentors are ready.
Judge whether each mentor can carry the season promise, then attach proof and a return pass to that call.
Treat the larger signup list as readiness proof, since growth shows the club has enough strength.
questions.explanation: The score is too thin unless it is tied to ability under the real promise. The head coach choice borrows rank, but rank does not show whether mentors can deliver.

questions.prompt: After a restaurant group misses an opening, leaders find that staff got warm praise but no one changed roles before launch. Which earlier step failed?
choices: The owners judged the chef's style instead of the dining promise, so they should redo the postmortem around personality fit.
The late gap proves the calendar was too loose, so they should set the opening day first and choose staff afterward.
The staffing pass stopped at praise; it did not produce coaching, a role move, or a new hire before the opening rush.
questions.explanation: A people pass has to lead to an action. The calendar answer has the timing backward; a firmer day does not repair a staffing call that produced no change.

questions.prompt: A disaster-relief nonprofit puts medical, logistics, and supply programs under one expansion lead because the growth story is clear. What maps from Honeywell?
choices: Let the national director carry all programs, since one senior title can keep the expansion aligned across relief teams.
Launch the programs together and wait for the first field reports to reveal which relief stream lacks depth.
Split the expansion by different operating demands and prove capable people exist for each relief stream before launch.
questions.explanation: The nonprofit has different loads inside one story, like Honeywell's portfolio. Waiting for field strain is late proof; depth should be matched before the promise hardens.

questions.prompt: When a university lab approves a new research direction but has no prepared lead for the hard part, what should happen?
choices: Revise the new direction around the missing lead, since the lab has no ready capacity for the hardest part.
Use grant interest as the proof, since outside demand makes the lab's staffing gap less urgent this term.
Set the submission deadline first, then ask the current team to stretch into the leadership gap before grants close.
questions.explanation: A new direction that lacks a ready lead is not sound yet. Grant interest is tempting proof, but demand does not fill the role the lab lacks.

questions.prompt: During a hospital staffing pass, every supervisor rates their backup as ready, yet weekend coverage keeps failing. What is actually wrong?
choices: The staffing pass aims at the wrong ward, so the hospital should move attention to the unit with the loudest complaints.
The ratings need candid calibration against coverage evidence before the weak backups hide inside the staffing path.
The senior nurse should endorse the ratings, so weekend teams know the readiness call has official backing.
questions.explanation: Inflated ratings hide the risk in the staffing path. The senior endorsement may feel stabilizing, but it accepts the same weak evidence with a stronger title.

questions.prompt: Suppose a community theater wants future directors to come from inside its own cast and crew. What lesson maps from Procter & Gamble?
choices: Choose the larger season now, because ambition will reveal which cast members grow fastest under pressure.
Build internal role paths that make future directors ready before each season depends on their judgment.
Ask an admired theater to lend a director, since outside prestige can make the first season easier.
questions.explanation: P&G shows the value of a long internal pipeline. The borrowed director may solve a season, but it does not build the theater's own prepared successors.

questions.prompt: The school district budget assumes the same dispatch staff can cover a new bus route. No one has named the capacity gap. What should change?
choices: Cut or staff the bus promise now, before the budget counts capacity the district has not proved for that route.
Let last year's balanced budget stand as proof that the district can absorb the new route this fall without a staffing change.
Write a stronger service value for families, so staff behavior changes through language before funds move.
questions.explanation: The numbers cannot borrow staff strength that has not been matched to the route. Last year's balance is wrong proof; it settles money, not load.

questions.prompt: At a neighborhood co-op, the current coordinator handles every hard call while the group talks about adding a new site. What comes first?
choices: Name the members with real promise and give them preparation before the co-op depends on them for expansion.
Improve the annual summary so members see the store has a strong bench and a clear growth story before voting.
Let the current coordinator keep every hard call until the future expansion has a start month.
questions.explanation: Future strategy depends on prepared successors, not on one coordinator carrying every hard call. A cleaner summary sounds useful, but it is not readiness.

questions.prompt: Imagine a music festival rated its crew well, then failed when the backup stage lead quit. Which earlier people-process move was missing?
choices: Ask the festival director to send a clearer message, since the crew missed the warning about role depth before the final roster.
Compare crew ratings after the event closes, then let succession wait until the season roster is almost due and pressure is real.
Pair the crew's delivery score with who can step into each role for the live crew, then set a return before the roster is trusted.
questions.explanation: The missing move was reading performance with succession. The clearer-message answer treats the miss as communication, but the real gap is testable readiness.

reviewCards.front: Why is a strong performance rating too thin by itself?
reviewCards.back: A rating looks backward. Execution needs a judgment about whether the person can carry a real promise, with proof that can return and be corrected.

reviewCards.front: What does Honeywell add to the people-process lesson?
reviewCards.back: Honeywell shows that one talent list can be too simple for a diversified industrial portfolio. Depth has to match the operating demand in each business.

reviewCards.front: When does a people pass count as more than appraisal?
reviewCards.back: It counts when it produces an action: development, reassignment, replacement, or a visible successor path. Without action, the score is not enough.

reviewCards.front: Why does Procter & Gamble's 1837 heritage matter here?
reviewCards.back: Its long internal leadership pipeline shows that prepared successors are built over time. Future strategy cannot depend on people who have not been readied.

reviewCards.front: What does candid calibration protect?
reviewCards.back: It keeps inflated ratings from hiding staffing risk. The aim is not cruelty; it is proof clear enough to change the path before the business trusts a weak promise.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use Staff the Promise Before Budget when a goal depends on a person whose capacity has not been proved. Ask who carries the promise, what proof shows readiness, and when the answer returns. The skill works only if the answer can change the staffing path.

ifThenPlans.context: Question the strong rating.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a strong rating carries a new promise, then staff the promise before budget by requiring readiness proof before the score is trusted.

ifThenPlans.context: Split the broad portfolio.
ifThenPlans.plan: If one talent list covers unlike businesses, then staff the promise before budget separately for each demand.

ifThenPlans.context: Expose the bench gap.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a future choice lacks a prepared successor, then staff the promise before budget before the strategy hardens.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Audit one staffing artifact for 20 minutes: cross-out every role that lacks readiness proof before the budget trusts it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, measure one number: how many hard promises have a prepared successor and a return pass. Improve the weakest one before adding a new promise.
