chapters.title: The Strategy Process: Making the Link with People and Operations
chapters.hook: 1971 put cheap fares on trial: if route, fleet, turnaround, and culture did not fit, the fare failed.
chapters.counterintuition: A broad strategy can feel bold because no one has to lose anything yet. It becomes real when the tradeoff, the capable lead, the budget line, and the first signal can all be checked.
chapters.tryThisNow: Watch one live priority for 10 minutes; move one note beside its budget line, then write the first gap you saw.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A strategy is ready only after the offer names its tradeoff and capable lead. The budget line and first signal must point to the same tested choice.

breakdown.fastRead:
1971 is the number Henri writes beside the fare. Southwest Airlines' 1971 low-cost model depended on route, fleet, turnaround, and culture choices that reinforced one another. Cheap fare was not the whole idea. Fit was.

Henri wants his own low-price claim to hold after the first buyer says yes. A sharper line will not do it. The claim has to refuse something. If custom options slow the turn, they do not belong. If no budget moves, the claim is still soft. A decision is a budget with a name and a return point.
breakdown.deepRead:
Fit works because it makes the promise pay its own bill. The outside offer has to match the inside path, the lead who can carry it, and the signal that will show trouble early. That feels slower than a broad yes. It is faster than a miss.

The computer case gives Blair the same rule. Dell built a direct-to-customer computer model during the 1980s and 1990s, and that model depended on supply-chain speed. Direct was not just a cleaner sales channel. It made the inside of the company prove that the order path could move as fast as the offer sounded.

Henri borrows that order. He writes the customer claim first, then asks which internal fact would make it false. Can orders move fast enough? Can a low fare survive the choices under it? Customers do not buy intent. They buy the delivered thing. No pass yet. Until budget, skill, and a visible signal line up with the customer claim, the market story is still a draft.

The short list matters. Too many priorities let each group keep its favorite add-on, and the operating base absorbs the conflict until a number is missed. Few priorities are load control, not a neat style.

The hidden bet is the last danger. If Henri assumes spare capacity, easy skill transfer, or late overtime, he puts that belief where others can see it. Say the bet early. Then the business can change it before money hardens around it.
breakdown.fullRead:
A chip case puts pressure on old loyalty. During the 1980s, Intel moved weight from memory chips toward microprocessors. Andy Grove and Gordon Moore are the named figures tied to that memory-to-microprocessor shift. The lesson is not that old bets are foolish. Old bets may have built the company. The danger is that they keep taking cash after the market has moved.

Study can become delay. When evidence hurts, one more read can feel careful, and sometimes care is right. But a strategy pass, the formal choice about direction, has to end in decisions. No call, no learning. If the old bet keeps capacity while the new fact waits outside the budget, the group has chosen without saying so.

Resources make the claim honest. A top item with no money, no staffing tradeoff, and no time set aside is still talk. Southwest shows this with fit. Dell shows it with speed. Intel shows it with market pressure. What has to move for the choice to be real?

Resource allocation is not a paperwork step. It is the moment the ledger shows whether the priority has weight. If money and staffing do not move, the priority is only a label. No blame is needed. The gap is information.

People are not an afterthought. A market choice is incomplete until it asks whether the business has the skill and judgment to carry the hard part. This is not a personality contest. It is a skill question. If the low-cost model needs fast turns, someone has to protect them. If the direct model needs supply-chain speed, someone has to make that path visible.

Henri uses that as his filter. He asks one thing: what would make the goal false when the first signal comes back? A hidden assumption is not a sin. It is a risk that has not been named yet. Once it is in view, budget can move, a priority can die, or a weak skill can be faced before the customer feels it.

The Southwest case is more than a cheap-fare story. Southwest Airlines began service in 1971, and its low-cost model tied the route map, fleet choice, quick turns, and culture into one system. Copy one visible choice and ignore the rest, and the model loses its force. Fit starts at the fare, not at the speech.

The move is not for every call. Do not bury a small reversible trial in months of study. Use it when the stakes are large, resources are scarce, or an old bet still has status. It costs comfort. It asks a favored item to lose money, a loved old bet to face a changed fact, and a clean story to name the skill it lacks. Skipping fit spends scarce capacity on a hope. Use it with care. Then stop.

examples.title: Henri Prices The Late Save
examples.scenario: The late save costs strategy lead Henri the clean story. The fare target has held, but cheap price gathered choices that fought each other. He needs a case where low cost lived as linked choices. Southwest Airlines began service in 1971, and its low-cost model depended on route, fleet, turnaround, and culture reinforcing one another. One blue mark circles the missed line. The catch held, barely.
examples.whatToDo: Price the skipped fit first. Henri cuts any add-on that makes route, fleet, or turnaround fight the low-cost model before the late save becomes habit.
examples.whyItMatters: Count the cost of the miss. A fare can survive one late catch, but the model stays weak until the choices under it reinforce one another.

examples.title: Blair Names The Slow Step
examples.scenario: The inside path is too slow when a buyer reaches launch lead Blair before the senior group feels the problem. The computer case makes the gap plain. Dell built a direct-to-customer computer model during the 1980s and 1990s, and the model depended on supply-chain speed. "What stayed slow?" Blair asks. "The path inside." The move half-works. The sales channel changed; the inside pace did not.
examples.whatToDo: Start with the buyer's wait, then name the slow step inside. Blair ties the direct offer to the supply-chain speed it needs before adding demand.
examples.whyItMatters: Listen to the delay because it shows why the move works. Customers feel the path, not the intent behind the channel, before any inside story matters.

examples.title: Clara Moves The Old Bet
examples.scenario: What should the first market fact change? Strategy lead Clara catches the weak signal while the old emphasis still holds the cash. She needs a case where market pressure changed the old emphasis. Intel's 1980s memory-to-microprocessor shift moved emphasis away from memory chips. The cursor blinked. Clara makes the fact touch the funding line, and the old bet loses cover.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what the first market fact would change. Answer by putting it against the funded choice and naming which old claim loses cover.
examples.whyItMatters: Pay the price while the signal is early. A market fact has not changed the strategy until it changes the resource choice.

examples.title: Remi Sets The Speed Bar
examples.scenario: "No pass until the speed has a capable lead." General manager Remi sets the bar. The market read says buyers will like direct orders, but inside skill arrives late. The computer case gives the standard teeth. Dell built its direct-to-customer computer model during the 1980s and 1990s, and supply-chain speed made the model work. Remi catches the gap just before approval.
examples.whatToDo: Name the speed lead before approval. If that name is missing, hold the choice until skill is shown against the direct offer.
examples.whyItMatters: Block the wish before buyers feel it. A market story without skill hides the gap until approval makes it harder to fix.

examples.title: Henri Keeps The Label Open
examples.scenario: Keep the label open. Strategy lead Henri is cutting the extra priority because the earlier ask missed its return point. Before the cut, the low-price claim had a label and no budget shift. Once the cut is made, the label stays open until money moves. He needs a case where the low price was a linked system. Southwest Airlines began service in 1971, and its low-cost model rested on choices that fit. The page edge catches his thumb. The answer stays unresolved.
examples.whatToDo: Move the budget line or cut the item. Do not let a priority keep its title when no resource has moved to protect the low-cost choice.
examples.whyItMatters: Refuse to call the claim real yet. Without a resource shift, the first hard tradeoff will expose the gap and make the label false.

examples.title: Clara Makes The Call
examples.scenario: Delay costs the choice its force. At the return point, strategy lead Clara starts with the choice itself. No further study is due; the call is. The chip case gives her the return point. Intel's 1980s memory-to-microprocessor shift shows why old emphasis cannot keep equal cover after market pressure changes. She names the changed fact and moves funding toward the newer bet. It works, and the old emphasis loses status.
examples.whatToDo: Name the cost of delay. Clara records the funding shift, names the capacity strain to watch, and refuses another read until the choice has moved.
examples.whyItMatters: Count what study protects. More reading can shield the old bet; changed demand matters only when it forces a decision the business can act on.

questions.prompt: Your product group has studied a weak market signal for weeks while an old line still keeps scarce engineering time. What is the single best next action?
choices: Keep the comparison running until the group can defend a cleaner read from the weak market and avoid a premature cut.
Let engineering carry both lines through the quarter, then look again once capacity strain is visible.
Make the capacity call now, name who carries it, and set the return point for the first evidence.
questions.explanation: Weeks of study have become delay while the old line keeps capacity. Carrying both lines sounds careful, but it lets engineering avoid the choice.

questions.prompt: A retailer finds buyers for a new service and treats demand as proof the chain can serve it. Which response best fits?
choices: Treat buyer interest as the hard evidence and let store gaps surface after launch, when demand is no longer theoretical.
Match the market bet to what stores can do and a visible delivery measure before launch gets approved.
Set the launch window first and ask store teams to close the delivery gap during rollout.
questions.explanation: Buyer interest does not prove delivery. Setting the launch window first starts motion, but it skips the inside skill test.

questions.prompt: During a sales surge, a regional unit adds many initiatives because growth feels like proof of strength. What happens next?
choices: The sales surge settles the capacity question, so the broader list can carry lighter scrutiny while results stay strong.
The unit narrows too soon, cutting useful bets before any strain has enough time to appear.
The crowded list eats capacity, so the few vital items lose force before growth proves real strength.
questions.explanation: Growth can hide load; it does not prove the unit can carry every added item. The lighter-scrutiny answer treats the wrong evidence as settled.

questions.prompt: Suppose a clinic approves a new care model but never tests who can carry the operating change. Which principle is broken?
choices: The direction passed before capable leadership was tested against the hard operating change it would carry.
The clinic weighs skill too early, before the patient need has enough external support.
The clinic stretches the people question too far by requiring every role in the building to be named first.
questions.explanation: Skill belongs inside the strategy pass, not after it. The every-role answer is too broad; the issue is who can carry the hard change.

questions.prompt: Your warehouse assumes overtime will cover a new delivery claim, but the assumption stays unspoken. What should happen before targets lock?
choices: Attach the delivery claim to a reward phrase, so supervisors hear the behavior expected before targets lock.
Bring the overtime bet into view and pick the signal that will show whether it holds before targets lock.
Wait for the first missed number, then decide whether overtime was the weak link behind the gap.
questions.explanation: Hidden assumptions become later misses. The reward phrase changes language around behavior, but it leaves the overtime bet buried.

questions.prompt: A discount repair service keeps its low price while adding custom options that slow the basic job. Which move best fits?
choices: Hand the low-price goal to staff once the message sounds simple enough to guide daily choices without more tradeoffs.
Cut the options that fight the low-cost system, even when each added choice looks attractive alone.
Add the options now and search for savings later, after demand shows which extras matter.
questions.explanation: Southwest teaches fit among tradeoffs, not a cheap message handed downward. The later-savings choice starts with strain and hopes to fix it later.

questions.prompt: Consider a software firm that keeps funding an old tool because it once defined the company, while demand shifts. Why change course now?
choices: Changed market evidence should challenge the old funding choice now, before old status consumes more capacity.
The old tool needs a more ambitious story, so the firm can defend its status while the new demand matures through this cycle.
The firm should wait until a side team proves the new demand is easier to serve and cheaper to fund.
questions.explanation: Intel shows changed market facts confronting an old emphasis. The ambition choice adds energy to the old tool, but it avoids the operating shift.

questions.prompt: Your nonprofit calls a youth program top priority, but no budget line or staffing tradeoff moves. Which reading best fits?
choices: The priority is still soft because no budget or staffing tradeoff backs it yet.
The deadline is the main device, so money can wait until demand is clearer.
The program can stay approved if a later pass finds spare capacity before spending starts.
questions.explanation: Resource allocation is the test. The spare-capacity answer keeps approval ahead of the hard tradeoff, so the priority remains mostly talk.

questions.prompt: Imagine a furniture maker copies direct-to-customer language but leaves order speed unnamed. Which correction best follows?
choices: Rewrite the customer message so the direct offer sounds simple to buyers and staff.
Treat the channel as settled once buyer research shows people like direct orders.
Define the operating path that lets the direct offer stay fast enough to trust.
questions.explanation: Dell makes direct selling an operating design, not just channel language. The message rewrite may clarify the offer, but it does not create speed.

reviewCards.front: Why is the Southwest low-cost model more than cheap fare?
reviewCards.back: The fare depends on linked choices. Route, fleet, turnaround, and culture have to reinforce one another, or the low-cost model loses force.

reviewCards.front: What must a direct offer name?
reviewCards.back: It must name the operating path behind the promise. Dell's direct-to-customer model in the 1980s and 1990s depended on supply-chain speed.

reviewCards.front: What should changed market facts be allowed to move?
reviewCards.back: They should move the old emphasis while money and capacity can still shift. Intel's 1980s change shows why loyalty to the old bet is not enough.

reviewCards.front: Why should strategic priorities stay few?
reviewCards.back: A long list can overwhelm operating capacity. A short list makes the business choose which bets deserve money, skill, and attention now.

reviewCards.front: How does funding expose a false priority?
reviewCards.back: If no budget line, staffing tradeoff, or time moves, the priority is still soft. Resource allocation shows whether the choice has become real.

reviewCards.front: Why is skill part of the strategy process?
reviewCards.back: The business has to know who can carry the hard change. The question is not personality; it is whether skill and judgment match the choice.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use one live priority as a fit ledger. Write the customer offer, the tradeoff it requires, the capable lead, the budget line, the visible signal, and the return point. If one line is blank, the priority is still a draft.

ifThenPlans.context: A customer claim wins support; then the delivery path stays unnamed.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the path is unnamed, then move the fit ledger to the speed it needs and the name that can carry it.

ifThenPlans.context: A market signal changes; then the old budget still holds.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old budget still holds, then move the fit ledger to the funded item that must lose cover.

ifThenPlans.context: A low-cost choice passes; then attractive extras keep returning.
ifThenPlans.plan: If extras keep returning, then move the fit ledger to the first item that fights the low-cost choice and cut it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Teach one other person for 10 minutes: move one live priority across a one-page fit ledger and explain which line fails first.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ahead of your standing weekly meeting, if a current priority lacks a budget line, a capable lead, or a return point, then move it back to draft and cut one weaker item.

memorableLines.text: Fit starts at the fare, not at the speech.
A decision is a budget with a name and a return point.
Skipping fit spends scarce capacity on a hope.

chapters.title: How to Conduct a Strategy Review
chapters.hook: What did Cisco have to ask after each smart technology deal looked worth doing?
chapters.counterintuition: A strong strategy story is still weak if no one can show how the business will carry it. The harder move is to make the story answer to people, money, and the return line before approval.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write this line on one live proposal, then say it out loud: "Who owes the operating proof, and by what day?"
chapters.keyTakeaway: Do not accept a strategy until the table can name who carries the hard part, which proof returns, how money ties to action, and when drift will show.

breakdown.fastRead:
What makes a Cisco-style technology deal ready after the logic sounds right? Cisco's technology acquisitions, repeated deals that required integration routines and strategic fit judgments, make the answer plain. The deal story is only one half. The other half is the path that absorbs the acquired capability, which means the habits and handoffs that make the new thing usable.

A strategy pass has to press on that path before money hardens. Name the person who carries the hardest part. Put the key proof where the group can see it. Set the return line early. No return, no proof.

That is the shift. The table is not there to admire a neat case. It is there to ask whether the operating path can answer the strategy. Make the operating path answer first.
breakdown.deepRead:
The mechanism is simple: a strategy gets real when the hard part has a name, a visible proof point, and a return line. Without those three, polite assent can hide a weak path until the budget is already spent. The price of polite agreement is late drift with money already spent.

Use this with care. A small trial that can be reversed may need speed more than a heavy pass. A crisis may need one person to act and explain later. This move costs time, candor, and some comfort; use it when the choice will move money, people, or the operating path.

IBM's 1993 services shift, a move toward services and integrated solutions, shows why the questions must reach below the claim. A services promise changes the business only if the model under it changes too. More ambition would not solve that gap. The table has to ask whether the customer value, the people, and the daily path fit the new promise.

General Electric's structured business reviews during its 1981 to 2001 chief executive era add a second pressure. GE's 1990s operating review practice did not treat a polished case as proof. The assumptions had to be defended before money moved. The question under each claim was plain: what has to be true for this to hold?

Candor is the hinge. It is not noise or a public fight. It is the choice to let weak evidence speak while it is still cheap to use. A weak strategy can survive warm nods; it has a harder time surviving named people, visible proof, and a return line.
breakdown.fullRead:
Cisco gives the most useful order. Start with fit, then ask how the acquired capability will be absorbed. Technology acquisitions can sound right at the deal table because the logic is clean: a needed capability, a market opening, a way to add strength. But Cisco's history points to the harder question. The deal is not ready until the integration routine can carry it.

That order reverses the default. Many groups want the broad yes first, then they hand the hard parts to staff. The problem is not laziness. The problem is that deal logic feels complete before the operating path has spoken. Who owes whom what by when?

The people question comes early because strategy without capable hands is only a wish with better grammar. Do not ask for a hero. Ask who has the skill, reach, and judgment to carry the part most likely to break. If no name can stand beside that part, the pass has found the gap before the customer does.

The fact question comes next. Generic market talk is too soft to guide action. A rival, a customer shift, or a changed need has to be named in plain words. Without that, the group can sound alert while still aiming at fog. The proof must be visible enough that a later return can show whether the claim held.

Then tie the number to the path. Financial logic is not false just because it is neat, but a number with no action under it becomes budget fiction. The table should be able to say which action makes the number true. If the action is missing, the number has no legs.

Milestones make drift visible. They are not clerical marks. They give the group a way to catch a miss while correction is still small. The return line should be close enough to make someone uncomfortable and clear enough that the answer cannot hide inside status talk.

IBM keeps the scope honest. A move toward services and integrated solutions was not a call for a louder slogan. It asked whether the business model matched the customer promise. When the old path and the new promise do not fit, the pass has to force the mismatch into the open.

General Electric's 1981 to 2001 review era keeps the tone honest. Disciplined dialogue is not a ritual for senior people. It is the habit of making assumptions carry weight before money is committed. A group that cannot state what must be true has not earned the right to spend as if it knows.

The move fails when it becomes theater. If people learn that candor is punished, the return line will fill with safe words. If every small choice gets the same heavy treatment, the business slows down and learns to avoid the table. Use the pass for bets that matter. Then make the answer short enough to read.

Write the return line before approval. The line should name the person, the proof, the action under the number, and the day the answer comes back. No one needs a longer speech. They need the day beside the name on the pass page.

examples.title: Bailey Sets The Return
examples.scenario: The deal sponsor asks what Cisco's technology acquisitions still owe once the case works. Bailey answers before approval: the acquired capability needs integration routines, not only a fit argument. A blue line sits under integration routines. Bailey sets the return for the absorption proof, but the answer is not back yet.
examples.whatToDo: When the deal case sounds finished, write the person, the absorption proof, and the return line before the pass can close.
examples.whyItMatters: When the return is still unmet, the group can see the open risk. Deal logic has not proved that Cisco-style absorption can work.

examples.title: Bailey Misses Absorption
examples.scenario: Bailey is already routing the acquired technology to teams. She treats Cisco's technology acquisitions as deal logic and skips the integration routines proof. The miss is plain: fit sounded right; no one can show how the capability will be absorbed.
examples.whatToDo: When absorption is vague, stop the pass. Write the routine before routing more work.
examples.whyItMatters: When fit hides capability, the miss moves downstream. The deal was not ready.

examples.title: Ophelie Catches The Model
examples.scenario: The proof comes back weak. Ophelie stops approval before it hardens: the services promise is running on the old path. IBM's 1993 services shift, a move toward services and integrated solutions, gives her the test. Name the model gap and make the owner bring back proof before the pass closes.
examples.whatToDo: When the old model carries the new promise, name it. Write who must prove the service path before approval holds.
examples.whyItMatters: When ambition outruns the path, say so. IBM shows that a services shift needs a business model that can carry it.

examples.title: Kyle Traces The Rival
examples.scenario: Money is already aimed at fog when Kyle opens the pass page again. The market line had said customers were shifting, but no rival or customer move had been named. General Electric's structured business reviews during its 1981 to 2001 chief executive era give Kyle the standard: defend assumptions before money moves. A cold coffee ring marks the page. The return is set, not met.
examples.whatToDo: When market talk stays generic, count the cost first. Write the specific rival, the customer shift, and the proof due back.
examples.whyItMatters: When a rival is unnamed, skipped discipline spends money on fog. GE's standard makes assumptions answer before funding hardens.

examples.title: Isaac Feels The Cost
examples.scenario: A return point tied to integration routines makes the budget number testable when Isaac enters the partner pass. He arrives to a slower path because Cisco's technology acquisitions budget now has an absorption action under it. The preferred add-on waits, and the move works cleanly.
examples.whatToDo: Before Isaac backs the add-on, write the pass note: which integration routine happens next, who owns the proof, and the date he will test the number again.
examples.whyItMatters: Because the routine has a milestone, the budget is no longer fiction. The cost is delay; the gain is a number that can be tested.

questions.prompt: During a museum expansion pass, several actions look useful. Which comes first, and why?
choices: Name the person skilled enough to carry the hardest change and make that name part of the expansion pass before approval.
Let the board chair approve the staffing story, since the title can settle who should carry the expansion before staffing is tested.
Map every museum role in detail before visitor demand is discussed, so no staffing gap can remain hidden.
questions.explanation: The expansion is not ready until skill is tied to the hard part. The board-chair answer borrows rank, but a title does not prove capacity.

questions.prompt: After factory leaders funded a new line, the first weak assumption surfaced too late. Which earlier step failed?
choices: The launch note did not make the growth aim clear enough to crews before the purchase.
The most senior engineer was not given sole power to settle assumptions before funds moved.
The business put money behind the claim before managers had tested its assumptions in hard dialogue.
questions.explanation: GE's lesson is to test assumptions before money moves. A clearer note sounds useful, but the failure was not weak wording.

questions.prompt: When a school district pass ends with warm agreement, a weak staffing case survives. Why did that happen?
choices: Polite assent kept the staffing weakness safe when early strain should have been treated as useful evidence.
The superintendent did not challenge every department in public, so the district could not prove toughness before staff weighed evidence.
The staffing case lacked a higher-ranked sponsor who could make agreement feel final to the district.
questions.explanation: Candor lets weak evidence surface while it can still help. Public toughness over-corrects; heat is not the same as useful truth.

questions.prompt: Your youth soccer club says participation is growing, so its travel plan must be sound. What maps best?
choices: Treat the larger signup count as proof that the travel plan can carry more teams this season.
Ask the league director to approve the plan, since outside standing can settle the club's market read.
Name the rival clubs and family shifts that explain demand before the club commits travel resources.
questions.explanation: Growth alone is too vague to guide action. The director option borrows status, but the club needs specific rivals and customer shifts.

questions.prompt: A software deal looked clever, then bogged down after closing. Which earlier gap best explains the failure?
choices: The sponsor should have handed the deal to staff once the strategic fit sounded persuasive and the closing path looked clear.
The pass proved the deal made sense but failed to prove the acquired technology could be absorbed.
The team should have delayed all deal talk until every post-close workflow was fully designed.
questions.explanation: Cisco's case makes absorption part of the strategy pass. The staff-handoff answer is tempting, but it drops the hard capability question.

questions.prompt: Before a city budget passes, the totals balance but no service action is named. Which priority is right?
choices: Let finance certify the totals first, then ask service teams to choose actions after funding lands.
Tie the budget number to the operating action that would make the service result true.
Move the deadline earlier, since the real problem is that service teams may drift after approval.
questions.explanation: The number needs an action under it. The earlier-deadline choice uses a real tool, but it targets timing while the budget lacks a path.

questions.prompt: A clinic rolls out a new intake path and learns about drift only after patients complain. What was missing?
choices: The clinic praised the intake change without tying rewards to the staff behavior it wanted.
The clinic should have studied the intake path longer before exposing patients to any change and naming an early return.
The clinic lacked a near return point that would have shown the intake drift while it was small.
questions.explanation: A milestone catches drift early. The rewards answer sounds related, but it aims at culture while the miss came from no early return.

questions.prompt: If a hardware firm copies IBM's 1993 move toward services, what question should the table press?
choices: Whether the firm can state a bolder services ambition that sounds large enough for customers.
Whether the business path can deliver services and integrated solutions, not just claim them.
Whether customer language should be rewritten so the new services push sounds simpler.
questions.explanation: IBM's shift asks whether the model can carry the services promise. Bolder ambition tempts, but it leaves the operating mismatch untouched.

questions.prompt: Suppose a grant team loves a clean proposal but has not named the beliefs holding it up. What should happen first?
choices: Ask what must prove true for the proposal to work, then make those beliefs visible before approval.
Judge which grant writer sounds most confident, since personality often reveals who will carry the proposal.
Freeze approval until the team can remove every uncertain belief from the proposal.
questions.explanation: The proposal rests on hidden assumptions. The confidence answer aims at personality, but the useful move is to expose the beliefs the plan relies on.

reviewCards.front: What does Cisco add to a deal discussion?
reviewCards.back: A deal must show how the acquired capability will be absorbed. Strategic fit is not enough until the integration routine can carry the work.

reviewCards.front: What does IBM's 1993 services shift force a group to ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the operating model matches the services promise. More ambition cannot fix a path that cannot deliver integrated solutions.

reviewCards.front: What did General Electric's structured passes put under pressure?
reviewCards.back: They put assumptions under pressure before money moved. A polished case had to defend what must be true, not only sound convincing.

reviewCards.front: Why do people requirements belong in a strategy pass?
reviewCards.back: A strategy is not executable until someone capable can carry the hard part. The people question is proof of readiness, not a staffing afterthought.

reviewCards.front: When does a budget number become fiction?
reviewCards.back: It becomes fiction when no operating action supports it. The number has to point to what changes, who carries it, and when evidence returns.

reviewCards.front: What does candor protect during the pass?
reviewCards.back: Candor protects early useful truth. Polite agreement can let weak claims survive until drift is costly, while a near return point exposes trouble sooner.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning a strategy claim into one line that can answer later. Write who carries the hard part, what proof returns, which action supports the number, and the day it comes back. The line should be short enough for everyone at the table to read.

ifThenPlans.context: A Cisco-style deal has one attractive fit number but no absorption measure.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a Cisco-style deal has one attractive fit number but no absorption measure, then write the return line with the one integration result due back.

ifThenPlans.context: A budget has one target number but no action under it.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a budget has one target number but no action under it, then write the return line with the one action that makes the number true.

ifThenPlans.context: A market claim cites one growth number but no rival or customer shift.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a market claim cites one growth number but no rival or customer shift, then write the return line with the one outside fact to verify.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the next strategy call, write this exact line in 10 minutes: "I will ask who owes the operating proof, what number returns, and by what day."
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the first weekly strategy meeting you already attend, observe one live strategy pass for 20 minutes, then note the first place a number, person, or return line is missing.

memorableLines.text: The price of polite agreement is late drift with money already spent.
Who owes whom what by when?
Write the return line before approval.

chapters.title: The Operations Process: Making the Link with Strategy and People
chapters.hook: Retail lead Hayes brakes at a red light after a store misses stock the budget said was safe.
chapters.counterintuition: A clean target can hide a weak operating path. You do not prove strategy by stating it. You prove it when a named person, a visible number, a tradeoff, and a return can answer soon.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before your first status scan today, say one number: how many live handoffs lack a named return before money or staff move.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Strategy becomes real when the budget line can answer: who acts, what fact moves, what gives way, and when the group returns before the miss grows.

breakdown.fastRead:
Retail lead Hayes is still at the red light when the miss stops sounding like bad luck. The store was short of stock that the budget said would be there. He asks, "Who would have known soon enough to fix it?"

Walmart, the retailer with a 1962 first-store origin, makes the answer plain. Its scale rested on stores tied to distribution and inventory discipline. Size did not make the promise true.

The operations process, the path from annual strategy to near-term acts, has to turn the aim into something that answers back. Name the person, number, tradeoff, and return. Make the promise answer back. Scale does not prove discipline; discipline earns scale.
breakdown.deepRead:
A budget line earns trust only when it can answer soon. The operations process is not a stack of forms; it is the way an annual aim becomes near-term acts, with a person, a fact, a tradeoff, and a return. A budget is a promise with money attached.

Dell, the Austin-based company built around build-to-order operations and fast inventory turns, shows why the number must sit close to the choice. The number must fit. If build-to-order operations are the strategy, broad sales alone can smile while inventory turns start to slow.

Operations analyst Hunter puts it to Hayes in one line. "The target is loud," Hayes says. "The wrong number can still be loud," Hunter answers. That exchange matters because staff can chase a broad goal while the chosen model loses the working-capital edge it was meant to protect.

Finance lead Maddox brings the harder part. More growth can sound good, more service can sound good, and more inventory can sound good. The same people and money cannot fund every attractive aim. What gives way? If no answer comes back, the budget is asking one resource to serve two masters.

Return also guards behavior. Words lose. If rewards praise one conduct while culture language asks for another, the old conduct wins unless someone comes back to the facts. Honeywell post-1999 company, an industrial mix with aerospace and automation businesses plus materials, adds the same lesson across units. Business-unit lead Irene cannot treat one unit's promise as sealed until the needed handoff is named. The early signal is not disloyal. It is the first useful answer.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hayes wants the first fix to be one clean metric. That is too neat. One number with no person near it can be late, and one person with no number can tell a true story after the money is gone.

Walmart began with a first store in 1962, not a proof of scale. Its store base had to meet distribution flow and stock control before size could help. Hayes has to ask where the shelf promise first becomes visible, who will know, and when the return happens. A broader target cannot answer those questions by sounding urgent.

The retail case also blocks a common dodge. A clearer claim may calm the table, but it does not place stock or show where the miss begins. The aim has to sit on the path that fills the store. That path is where strategy stops being speech and becomes a hard promise.

Dell, an Austin-based company, sharpens the metric through build-to-order operations. If the model depends on fast inventory turns, the broad sales total can arrive with a smile on its face while the build flow is already strained. Hunter is not rejecting sales. He is asking whether the chosen proof is near enough to the strain.

A close measure still needs a tradeoff. Maddox can fund the Walmart add-on or protect the distribution and inventory promise, but not both with the same money. The cost is not just a cut. It is the loss of an easy yes, and that loss is why the smaller promise can stay honest.

Honeywell brings the cross-unit strain: in the post-1999 company, aerospace, automation, and materials sat inside one industrial portfolio. Each unit can sound ready while the handoff between them stays blank. The weak point may sit between units, not inside the unit with the best-sounding target. Irene's job is to keep that gap visible without pretending it is solved.

What if the signal is thin? Irene carries that harder case. If she demands a finished answer, people may wait until the answer is safe. If she lets a vague worry pass as truth, the path fills with fog. The useful move is narrower: say what is known, say what is not known, and set a return close enough to matter.

Rewards create another test. A group can ask for new conduct while still praising the old conduct. If the group never returns to see what changed, the culture line becomes cover. Behavior changed is the fact that counts.

This is how people, strategy, and operations reinforce one another. People choices ask who can carry the promise. Strategy asks which aim deserves scarce money. The operating path asks how soon reality can answer. Treat early bad news as data, and correction can still be cheap. Treat it as disloyal, and the first honest signal goes quiet.

examples.title: Hayes Traces The Recovered Miss
examples.scenario: The red bin is still on Hayes's screen when the stock miss is declared fixed. Treat it as the anchor, not the ending: the Walmart question moves from that bin to store operations, distribution and inventory discipline. Sam Walton opened Walmart's first store in 1962, yet Hayes treats the origin as a cost lesson: the promise worked only after someone paid for daily discipline.
examples.whatToDo: Hayes starts with a command: name the store promise, the person who can move it, the number that shifts first, and the return that proves it.
examples.whyItMatters: Hayes keeps the command harsh: do not let scale speak for the store. Turn the large aim into a small line that can fail early.

examples.title: Hunter Feels The Late Measure
examples.scenario: Operations analyst Hunter arrives from outside the approval group before Hayes lets the target pass. The cost is delay: the broad sales number still looks fine, but Dell, the Austin-based company, has build-to-order operations that no longer feel fast enough for fast inventory turns. "The model is moving faster than the measure," Hunter tells Hayes.
examples.whatToDo: Hunter names the cost first: skipping the closer measure lets Dell lose the early signal. He moves the number toward build flow and inventory turns.
examples.whyItMatters: Hunter warns that skipping this lets staff hit a broad number while the chosen model drifts. The measure has to carry the strategy, not trail it.

examples.title: Irene Holds The Handoff Open
examples.scenario: Business-unit lead Irene hears the mechanism fail at the transfer: automation waits on aerospace before anyone else sees why the portfolio target may not hold. Honeywell's post-1999 company is a diversified industrial portfolio with aerospace and automation businesses plus materials, so the gap is normal. The conference phone hums. "Name the handoff," Irene says.
examples.whatToDo: Irene uses the gap because the miss sits between units. She states the handoff, names who returns with the answer, and keeps the target open.
examples.whyItMatters: Irene keeps the answer open because partial truth is still useful. A false full answer would quiet the warning; a return keeps it live.

examples.title: Maddox Makes The Cut
examples.scenario: "What gives way if this stays?" Finance lead Maddox asks as Hayes pushes for the Walmart target. The answer is the useful add-on: Walmart's 1962 origin still points to distribution and inventory discipline. The sponsor must choose: fund the extra aim or protect the smaller promise that can answer soon.
examples.whatToDo: Maddox asks the question you would avoid: what leaves the list? He makes the sponsor name the cut before the budget line is treated as funded.
examples.whyItMatters: Maddox makes the cost visible. The move works because the attractive add-on is not free; losing it keeps the live promise honest.

questions.prompt: After the shelf miss, Hayes traces the stock target back to the point the expansion aim moved. Which absence made the target unable to answer early?
choices: No named person, live store number, or return had been set before the expansion aim moved ahead.
A distribution owner and live count were in place, but store teams were left out of the later return.
Store scale had already proved stock discipline, so the target mainly needed a cleaner growth story.
questions.explanation: Walmart's lesson is answerable discipline, not a cleaner claim. The scale-as-proof option tempts, but it accepts size before the store path can answer.

questions.prompt: During a budget pass, totals balance and the handout looks tidy, but no one can say what changes by month-end. What is wrong?
choices: Money has been approved without a tied action, named person, and milestone that would make it usable.
Finance should own the line because demand will show which function deserves the money once the target is live.
The balanced totals settle the first pass, so the only gap is which group receives the funds.
questions.explanation: Balanced math is not enough. The budget needs an act, a person, and a milestone; the spend-first choice delays the very part that makes it usable.

questions.prompt: A service group names a conduct promise once, then shifts reward talk to culture language and never returns to the conduct. What follows?
choices: Culture language will carry the change if rewards are described often and the conduct is praised at year-end by senior staff.
The promise should stay at culture level, since return points might make the message feel too narrow.
The promise weakens because no return shows whether rewards and daily conduct moved together after the first yes.
questions.explanation: A return keeps behavior from drifting. The culture-language choice sounds warm, but it lets words stand in for conduct evidence.

questions.prompt: When a builder sells from demand but still judges the cycle by broad sales as the build queue slows, what single move fits the model?
choices: Let line staff set finer measures after the sales target has guided the first operating cycle.
Keep sales as the main proof, since demand volume suggests the build path is drawing orders from the right customers.
Move the metric toward build flow and inventory turns, where strain appears before sales hides it.
questions.explanation: Dell's case ties the number to the chosen model. The sales-proof choice uses a real figure, but it sits too far from build-to-order strain.

questions.prompt: Early bad news reaches a steering group, and a senior voice treats the person who raised it as disloyal. What is the better read?
choices: The speaker's loyalty should be handled apart from the signal, so staffing judgment can close before the group weighs the warning.
The warning is useful data because people choices, strategy, and operating results are testing the same promise.
Full-year support is stronger evidence, since early strain can make the strategy look smaller than the full-year target.
questions.explanation: Early strain tests the link among people, strategy, and operations. The loyalty choice aims at the speaker and loses the useful signal.

questions.prompt: Two functions set launch timing for a rollout, but neither states the handoff one needs from the other before the first release step. Which risk is live?
choices: The transfer belongs inside the receiving function, so the other group can stay focused on its own timing.
A hidden cross-team dependency can break the launch even when both functions accept the same timing line.
The agreed timing can stand as proof for now, since the handoff can be named inside launch prep.
questions.explanation: The danger is the unnamed dependency. The timing answer sounds orderly, but a shared calendar cannot carry a transfer no one stated.

questions.prompt: Inside a diversified industrial company, aerospace sounds ready while automation waits on an unnamed shared input. What is the diagnosis?
choices: The operating pass has not joined unit promises across the portfolio, so the shared input remains loose.
The aerospace gain gives enough evidence for the portfolio target while automation catches up with its own input.
The shared input can stay inside automation, since each unit should first prove its own promise.
questions.explanation: Honeywell's portfolio lesson is cross-unit coordination. The aerospace-only answer is too narrow because automation can still fail at the shared input.

questions.prompt: Your group accepts attractive growth goals while leaving the same people and money in place. What consequence should you expect?
choices: The larger scale will reveal the resource gap once demand rises, so an early tradeoff would narrow the aim.
The goals will fight for scarce people and money unless one aim gives something up early enough to be real.
The most popular target should claim the shared resource, because support reveals which goal matters most.
questions.explanation: Attractive goals still draw from finite resources. The scale answer accepts growth as proof, which is the shortcut this lesson rejects.

questions.prompt: Annual strategy wins wide support, yet no short-cycle signal will show drift while correction is still cheap. What move fits?
choices: Judge sponsor energy first, since the people link will show whether the broad aim has enough backing.
Keep the yearly aim intact until results close, because early signals can make the target feel smaller.
Break the annual aim into near-term promises that can reveal drift while there is time to adjust.
questions.explanation: The operating path turns the yearly aim into shorter promises so drift appears early. The sponsor answer points at people without creating the signal.

reviewCards.front: What does Walmart add beyond scale?
reviewCards.back: Size matters only after store operations, distribution, and inventory discipline can answer for the promise.

reviewCards.front: When does a budget become usable?
reviewCards.back: It becomes usable when money is tied to an action, a person, and a milestone. Balanced totals alone do not change conduct.

reviewCards.front: Why did Dell need measures near build flow?
reviewCards.back: Dell's build-to-order model needed measures close to inventory turns and build speed. Broad sales could look fine while the model strained.

reviewCards.front: What makes Honeywell a handoff case?
reviewCards.back: Its industrial portfolio spans aerospace, automation, and materials. One unit can sound ready while the needed transfer between units is still unnamed.

reviewCards.front: How should early bad news be treated?
reviewCards.back: Treat it as useful data about the link among people, strategy, and operations. Calling it disloyal removes the signal that could make correction cheap.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use one spoken line before a target passes. Say who acts, which fact moves, what gives way, and when the group returns. The line is small so weak promises cannot hide inside broad support.

ifThenPlans.context: If a budget balances but no action changes
ifThenPlans.plan: If a budget balances but no action changes, then say the proof line with the act, the person, the milestone, and the first return.

ifThenPlans.context: If one function waits on another function
ifThenPlans.plan: If one function waits on another function, then say the proof line with the handoff named before the target passes.

ifThenPlans.context: If early bad news sounds like blame
ifThenPlans.plan: If early bad news sounds like blame, then say the proof line by naming what the signal tests and who returns with the next fact.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Bolt this onto tomorrow's first calendar scan: say one live promise, its person, its number, and its return in 60 seconds.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Before your standing weekly operating review, run a 20-minute proof-line pass on one budget target, and cut any aim that lacks a tradeoff, a handoff, or a return.

memorableLines.text: Make the promise answer back.
Scale does not prove discipline; discipline earns scale.
A budget is a promise with money attached.
